The issue persists outside the training domain after a seven-year gap and can misdirect development choices such as classifier-free guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Generative precipitation nowcasting is a predictive video/world-model task, and the paper's sampling-bias analysis is transferable to video world model evaluation.
papers.title: Wet-Biased Data Pipelines Mislead the Training and Evaluation of Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.tldr: Wet-biased, target-dependent sampling can distort both generative precipitation-nowcasting training and evaluation, even reversing conclusions about forecast calibration.

papers.abstract: Expand-and-sparsify ($\texttt{EaS}$) representations lift an input to a much higher dimension through a linear map and keep only the $k$ largest coordinates. Existing theory builds that map at random and needs the expanded dimension to grow exponentially in the input dimension, which puts the construction out of practical reach. We ask what is gained by learning the map by gradient descent instead, and how that gain depends on how wide the expansion is. We sweep $73$ OpenML classification tasks and $48$ regression tasks under a protocol that holds the datasets, expanded dimensions, sparsity levels and splits fixed across every method, and we summarise each comparison by a median over datasets and a Wilcoxon signed rank test. We report four findings. First, learning the expansion helps most when the expansion is narrowest, and its advantage over a random map decays to nothing by the widest expansions we run, so a learned $\texttt{EaS}$ layer can be made small. Second, with the map learned, a top-$k$ representation that keeps at most a tenth of its coordinates is indistinguishable from a dense $\texttt{ReLU}$ layer of the same expanded dimension at every expansion factor we test, while GELU and SiLU are not. Third, when the representation is forced to be binary the sparse code is the better of the two, and the reason is that binarization costs it nothing while it costs the dense layer accuracy. Fourth, how sparse the representation can be is governed by how wide it is: the sparsity level that is free rises as the expansion grows, so there is no fixed limit on how sparse it can be. The regression tasks reproduce the first finding and qualify the second and third.
authors: Alireza Asghari, Parikshit Ram, Kaushik Sinha
bullets: Learned expansion maps outperform random ones most at narrow widths; the advantage disappears at the widest tested expansions.
Keeping at most 10% of coordinates can match a same-width dense ReLU layer, unlike GELU or SiLU, across tested expansion factors.
Under binary representations, sparse codes outperform dense ones because binarization does not reduce sparse-code accuracy.
The sparsity level that remains effectively free increases with expansion width, rather than being capped by a fixed limit.
Findings are based on 73 classification and 48 regression tasks; regression reproduces the learning benefit but qualifies some comparisons.
papers.selection_reason: Learned expand-and-sparsify representations with top-k sparsity are relevant to reducing computation in AI systems.
papers.title: On Learning Expand-and-Sparsify Representations
papers.tldr: Learning the expansion map makes sparse expand-and-sparsify representations practical, with narrower expansions benefiting most and allowable sparsity increasing with expansion width.

papers.abstract: Human-collected robot manipulation data often mix successful behavior with retries, pauses, recoveries, and failures. Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning (AC-BC) can exploit such mixed-quality data, but only if the conditioning signal is both accurately constructed from offline trajectories and effectively incorporated into the policy's action-vector-field prediction. Existing pipelines can weaken this signal by thresholding estimator-derived advantage scores into noisy conditions, and by routing conditions through prompts that weakly affect the action vector field. We introduce ALIGN, a condition-aligned AC-BC framework for vision-language-action policies. ALIGN directly predicts categorical pairwise conditions in the policy-facing label space and injects them into a DiT action expert through AdaRMS modulation fused with flow time. We evaluate ALIGN on deliberately mixed real-robot datasets for ARX X5 bowl stacking and Franka key hanging, each combining standard demonstrations with retry-heavy trajectories. ALIGN improves condition fidelity, strengthens conditional vector-field separability, and achieves 90.0% and 56.7% closed-loop success, compared with 56.7% and 33.3% for the strongest AC-BC baseline. These results indicate that aligning conditions from estimation to action prediction is an effective way to extract robust manipulation policies from data in which success, recovery and error coexist.
authors: Zechen Wang, Zhenqi Qiu, Houlong Xiong, Suohang Zhang, Yiyu Ren, Wanting Xu, Hongfei Niu, Chengyang He, Ge Sun, Ran Cheng, Qian Zhu
bullets: Addresses mixed-quality robot demonstrations containing successes, retries, recoveries, and failures.
Predicts categorical pairwise conditions directly in the policy-facing label space instead of thresholding estimated advantages.
Injects conditions into a DiT action expert using AdaRMS modulation fused with flow time.
Evaluated on mixed real-robot datasets for ARX X5 bowl stacking and Franka key hanging.
Achieves 90.0% and 56.7% closed-loop success, versus 56.7% and 33.3% for the strongest AC-BC baseline.
papers.selection_reason: AC-BC framework for VLA robot manipulation policies from mixed-quality data.
papers.title: ALIGN: Aligning Condition Estimation and Expression in Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning
papers.tldr: ALIGN improves advantage-conditioned behavior cloning by making quality conditions more accurate and more directly influence robot action prediction.

papers.abstract: Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation, interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight online memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.
authors: Guannan Lai, Zi-Yang Bai, Jun-Peng Jiang, Han-Jia Ye
bullets: Resource constraints can make existing memory methods ineffective, as irrelevant or ineffective retrieval consumes scarce context and reasoning capacity.
The key challenge is to estimate memory worth—not merely retrieve relevant experiences.
TokenWorth is a lightweight online framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback.
It uses the learned worth signal for both memory retrieval and bounded memory management.
Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and local/API deployments, it achieved the highest task success with the fewest output tokens among evaluated methods.
papers.selection_reason: Learns query-dependent memory worth for lifelong agents under tight memory and token budgets.
papers.title: Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints
papers.tldr: TokenWorth learns which experiences are worth retaining and retrieving, enabling more effective lifelong-agent adaptation under tight resource budgets.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can produce unsafe content, while output filtering intervenes only after synthesis. We investigate whether native generation signals enable early detection of unsafe and adversarial inputs. We find that classifier-free guidance exposes strong safety signals in conditional responses, accessible through compact statistics and linear readouts. Based on this finding, we propose Conditional Semantic Trajectory Interception (CSTI), which aggregates activation contrasts between conditional and unconditional responses at early checkpoints for calibrated risk detection. CSTI fits concept-specific detectors using canonical concept and safe examples, without attack samples, intermediate image decoding, or generator modification. Across five generators, four adversarial attack collections, and two general NSFW datasets, CSTI achieves the strongest overall performance among six baselines at a matched 5% FPR. Early interception reduces generation latency by over 60% on intercepted paths. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of native conditional responses for early safety interception.
authors: Yanchun Li, Yujin Wu, Gangkai Shen, Ming Yang, Li Zeng, Xianlong Wang, Hangtao Zhang, Shujuan Tian
bullets: Addresses the limitation of output filtering, which acts only after unsafe content is synthesized.
Uses contrasts between conditional and unconditional responses at early diffusion checkpoints with compact statistics and linear readouts.
Trains concept-specific detectors from canonical concept and safe examples, without attack samples.
Across five generators, four attack collections, and two NSFW datasets, it had the strongest overall performance among six baselines at 5% FPR.
Intercepting unsafe generations early reduced latency by over 60% on intercepted paths.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates early interception of unsafe inputs in text-to-image generation using native generation signals. This contributes to safety mechanisms in diffusion models and reduces generation latency.
papers.title: When Guidance Becomes a Guard: Early Interception of Unsafe Inputs in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.tldr: CSTI detects unsafe or adversarial text-to-image inputs early by analyzing classifier-free guidance signals, avoiding image decoding and generator changes.

papers.abstract: We study whether geometric relationships between conversation turns, memory texts, and queries can predict answer correctness before generation. We evaluate four memory implementations with dense or hybrid retrieval and one observation-summary comparator. We embed these texts in a shared space. A logistic classifier uses 25 features describing query proximity, memory-conversation correspondence, and conversation structure. On LongMemEval-small, pooled AUROC is 0.640 over 2,367 question-system pairs, below a question-difficulty baseline of 0.655. Performance varies by question type: geometry reaches 0.841 on single-session-assistant questions, but system identity alone reaches 0.826. After controlling for difficulty and identity, geometry adds no statistically established pooled improvement (delta = +0.002, 95% CI [-0.010, 0.014]). A fixed-store context-selection experiment finds higher accuracy with proximity-ranked memories than with random subsets, consistent with ordinary retrieval relevance. On LoCoMo, nearest-turn similarity has modest predictive value for single-hop questions and near-chance estimates for several other categories. Training uses correctness labels; prediction uses pre-answer features and no additional LLM generation call. The results characterize associations between memory representations and correctness, rather than establish a reliable deployment diagnostic. In particular, embedding proximity does not verify fact coverage or distinguish memory-construction, retrieval, and generation errors.
authors: Iliya Zhechev, Radoslav Ralev, Chris Coleman, Srijith Rajamohan, Jen Agarwal, Tyler Hutcherson, Simba Khadder
bullets: Evaluates four dense or hybrid retrieval systems plus an observation-summary comparator using shared-space embeddings.
A 25-feature logistic classifier reaches pooled AUROC 0.640, below a question-difficulty baseline of 0.655.
Geometry performs better for some question types, but adds no established pooled improvement after controlling for difficulty and system identity.
Proximity-ranked memory selection improves accuracy over random subsets, consistent with ordinary retrieval relevance.
Embedding proximity cannot verify fact coverage or distinguish memory-construction, retrieval, and generation errors.
papers.selection_reason: Studies geometric relationships in agent memory and retrieval for predicting answer correctness, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: The Geometry of Agent Memory: Forecasting Retrieval-Bound Memory Failures, and Characterizing Its Limits
papers.tldr: Geometric features of agent memory provide limited, non-robust prediction of answer correctness before generation and do not reliably diagnose memory failures.

papers.abstract: While VideoLLMs have made significant progress in understanding short video benchmarks, they often struggle to summarize long-form ones. This is mainly due to performance degradation caused by long-context prompts, the inherent difficulty of preserving temporal continuity and a lack of semantically rich concepts in event descriptions. To tackle these issues, this paper introduces the first recursive Video Language Summarization Model (RVLSM) designed for video processing and tailored to long-form video-to-text summarization. RVLSM recursively decomposes videos into semantically coherent segments and delegates chunk-level reasoning to VideoLLM sub-models and external tools. It employs (1) Semantic Temporal Decomposition (STD), which preserves temporal coherence and continuity through a scene-aware chunking strategy that dynamically partitions videos according to semantic boundaries, and (2) Adaptive Multimodal Tool Calling (AMTC), which ensures semantic richness of the summary via a routing mechanism that selectively invokes auxiliary modules such as action recognition, optical character recognition, automatic speech recognition, and object detection. Experiments on the VideoXum and MixTyVSum benchmarks show that RVLSM consistently improves over zero-shot VideoLLM baselines across multiple model settings and performance metrics, and is competitive with a state-of-the-art fine-tuned model for video-to-text summarization. Importantly, the named entities in the RVLSM's summaries align more closely with those detected in the ground-truth summaries than those detected by baseline and state-of-the-art methods, confirming the saliency of the event descriptions it generates.
authors: Alessia Intini, Lorenzo Vaiani, Enrico Chen, Luca Cagliero
bullets: Addresses VideoLLMs’ difficulties with long contexts, temporal continuity, and sparse event descriptions.
Uses Semantic Temporal Decomposition to split videos at meaningful scene boundaries while preserving continuity.
Uses Adaptive Multimodal Tool Calling to selectively invoke action recognition, OCR, ASR, and object detection.
Outperforms zero-shot VideoLLM baselines across VideoXum and MixTyVSum settings and metrics.
Generates summaries with named entities more closely aligned to ground-truth summaries and is competitive with a fine-tuned state-of-the-art model.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a recursive Video Language Summarization Model (RVLSM) designed for long-form video-to-text summarization. It employs semantic temporal decomposition and adaptive multimodal tool calling, improving long-video understanding.
papers.title: Long-form Video-to-Text Summarization using Recursive Language Models
papers.tldr: RVLSM improves long-form video summarization by recursively segmenting videos and selectively using multimodal tools to produce temporally coherent, semantically rich summaries.

papers.abstract: Expressive robot motion can improve naturalness, effectiveness, and perceived likability in human-robot interaction. When deployed on dynamically unstable platforms, however, reactive execution of expressive body motion may bring the robot to its stability limits, especially when expressivity is decoupled from physical control. In this paper, we present RoboMMT (Robot Modulated Motion Tracking), a modular control architecture that couples parameterized expressive motion synthesis, physics-based character control, and reactive adaptation to spatial interaction goals. Our approach trains a reference-conditioned tracking policy across a broad domain of expressivity, enabling it to faithfully realize the commanded motions while maintaining dynamic stability. Goal reactivity is achieved by training lightweight, task-specific interaction policies that modulate the reference generator's spatial goal-attraction point, with the stabilizing tracking policy kept in the loop. Evaluations on a quadruped and two humanoid robots show that the learned tracker remains stable and accurate across the entire modulation domain, whereas trackers trained without this coverage lose balance, tracking accuracy, or both. We show that layering closed-loop goal adaptation over this foundation enables interactive facing and pointing behaviors, while maintaining stable execution and comparable reference-tracking fidelity. The robot learns to proactively redistribute its weight and take corrective steps. Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated through real-robot experiments on a quadruped under heavy disturbances.
authors: Till Hielscher, Kai O. Arras
bullets: Addresses the challenge of executing expressive motion on dynamically unstable robots without sacrificing balance.
Combines expressive motion synthesis, physics-based control, and reactive goal adaptation in a modular architecture.
Trains a reference-conditioned tracker across a broad expressivity range to maintain stable, accurate motion execution.
Lightweight interaction policies adjust spatial goal attraction to support interactive facing and pointing while retaining tracking fidelity.
Demonstrated on quadruped and humanoid robots, with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a quadruped under heavy disturbances.
papers.selection_reason: Learning stable tracking of expressive robot motion with goal-reactive modulation.
papers.title: RoboMMT: Learning Stable Tracking of Modulated Expressive and Interactive Robot Motion
papers.tldr: RoboMMT enables robots to perform expressive, interactive motions while preserving accurate tracking and dynamic stability, including under real-world disturbances.

papers.abstract: Image-based spatial reasoning requires perception, decomposition, and inference, but the stage that limits accuracy can change during training. Answer-level rewards neither localize failures to individual stages nor provide discriminative group-relative feedback when all rollouts receive the same reward. Process supervision provides intermediate feedback, but fixed weights cannot adapt reward allocation to these changing bottlenecks. To address this gap, we propose CALIPER, an adaptive process-reward framework supported by SpatialTrace, a corpus of stage-decomposed spatial reasoning traces. CALIPER jointly estimates the associations between stage-wise reference coverage and answer correctness through within-group ridge regression, using these associations as utility proxies to gradually update reward weights. The resulting process reward supervises all rollout groups, including uniformly failing ones. Because utility estimates can become unreliable when answer-discriminative groups are scarce, a closed-loop harness monitors estimator reliability and validation performance to guide checkpoint rollback, rollout diversification, and early stopping. Extensive experiments across eight benchmarks and three backbones show that CALIPER achieves the highest mean under both one-shot and harness training, with consistent gains over fixed allocation across RL optimizers. Further analyses confirm the benefits of adaptive reward allocation and harness control, with favorable scaling in model/data size.
authors: Hailiang Yang, Shengchao Chen
bullets: Fixed answer-level rewards cannot localize failures, while fixed process-reward weights cannot adapt to changing bottlenecks.
CALIPER uses within-group ridge regression to estimate how stage-wise reference coverage relates to answer correctness and update reward weights.
It provides process supervision even when all rollout groups fail uniformly.
A closed-loop harness monitors estimator reliability and validation performance to trigger rollback, rollout diversification, or early stopping.
Experiments across eight benchmarks and three backbones report the highest mean performance for both one-shot and harness training, with consistent gains over fixed allocation.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses image-based spatial reasoning with a Policy-Adaptive Credit Assignment framework. The method involves stage-wise decomposition and utility estimation, which is relevant to spatial reasoning and geometric understanding.
papers.title: Policy-Adaptive Credit Assignment for Spatial Reasoning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.tldr: CALIPER adaptively reallocates process-level rewards to the spatial-reasoning stages most associated with answer correctness, improving training across benchmarks and backbones.

papers.abstract: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) localizes the image region described by a natural language expression, underpinning applications such as autonomous navigation, human-robot interaction, and medical image analysis. Under weak supervision, REC is challenged by the visual-linguistic semantic gap and the difficulty of inferring region-text correspondences from coarse image-level signals alone. Moreover, no single visual encoder captures all complementary properties---semantic alignment, fine-grained texture, and boundary awareness---while naively fusing multiple pretrained encoders yields heterogeneous, hard-to-reconcile representations. We propose LaMER, a weakly supervised REC framework that dynamically aggregates four frozen expert encoders through a language-conditioned Cross-Modal Routing Fusion module, adapting expert selection to each referring expression without instance-level bounding-box supervision. A Cell-Text Matching Head with Negative Anchor Augmentation, trained with a multi-objective loss combining contrastive, reconstruction, alignment, and load-balancing terms, further stabilizes optimization. LaMER achieves 77.67\%, 62.81\%, and 69.49\% Acc@IoU\(\geq 0.5\) on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, surpassing DViN and WeakMCN by up to 16.49 and 14.49 points, with ablations validating each component.
authors: Yu Yu Chang, Tzu-Hsuan Weng, Youssef Mohamed Amin, Mohaned Ahmed Elsayed, Hung-Hsuan Chen, Min-Te Sun, Sherine Shawky
bullets: Addresses the visual-linguistic gap and difficulty of learning region-text correspondences from image-level supervision.
Uses language-conditioned Cross-Modal Routing Fusion to dynamically select and combine four frozen visual encoders.
Adds a Cell-Text Matching Head with Negative Anchor Augmentation and a multi-objective training loss.
Reports 77.67% on RefCOCO, 62.81% on RefCOCO+, and 69.49% on RefCOCOg at IoU ≥ 0.5.
Ablations support the contribution of the proposed components; evaluation is limited to the reported REC benchmarks and weak-supervision setting.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes LaMER, a weakly supervised framework for Referring Expression Comprehension that uses a language-conditioned Cross-Modal Routing Fusion module. This contributes to multimodal fusion techniques for VLMs.
papers.title: LaMER: Language-Conditioned Multi-Expert Routing for Weakly Supervised Referring Expression Comprehension
papers.tldr: LaMER improves weakly supervised referring expression comprehension by routing language queries across complementary frozen visual experts without requiring bounding-box annotations.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation can transfer the reasoning capabilities of a strong teacher to a smaller student. However, distillation from a stronger teacher model faces two mismatches: its solutions may be difficult for a smaller student to imitate, and its token-level probabilities may be incompatible with, or even unavailable to, the student. Existing methods handle these settings through different forms of supervision. To this end, we propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD), a unified framework for distilling from any teacher that provides reasoning traces. The model to be distilled from, termed the external teacher, first provides a reasoning trace as privileged context, which can be generated in an offline fashion. The student generates rollouts without this context, while a copy of the student conditioned on it, serving as the self-teacher, scores the same rollouts in the student's own token space. BSD uses the resulting token-level guidance to adjust updates on unsuccessful rollouts, with a verifier providing the outcome signal. As the external teacher is queried only to produce text, the same training procedure applies to all teacher scenarios: shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers. Across these scenarios, BSD improves over the base model and outperforms baselines tailored to each scenario, offering a novel and unified pathway for distillation. Code is available: https://github.com/TUMLegalTech/Bridged-Self-Distillation
authors: Runsheng Chen (Technical University of Munich, Germany), Yihong Liu (LMU Munich, Germany, Munich Center for Machine Learning, Germany), Raoyuan Zhao (LMU Munich, Germany, Munich Center for Machine Learning, Germany), Michael A. Hedderich (LMU Munich, Germany, Munich Center for Machine Learning, Germany), Hinrich Sch\"utze (LMU Munich, Germany, Munich Center for Machine Learning, Germany), Matthias Grabmair (Technical University of Munich, Germany)
bullets: Addresses two challenges: teacher solutions may be hard to imitate, and teacher token probabilities may be incompatible or unavailable.
The external teacher supplies reasoning traces, which can be generated offline; the student then learns without access to those traces at rollout time.
A trace-conditioned copy of the student scores the student’s rollouts in the student’s own token space.
A verifier identifies unsuccessful rollouts, and BSD uses the self-teacher’s guidance to adjust their updates.
Works with shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed-API teachers, improving over the base model and scenario-specific baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a unified distillation framework for LLM reasoning traces, relevant to LLM training and model improvement.
papers.title: Bridged Self-Distillation for On-Policy Learning
papers.tldr: Bridged Self-Distillation transfers reasoning from diverse teachers to smaller students by using teacher-generated traces as context for a self-teacher that provides compatible token-level guidance.

papers.abstract: Animals build cognitive maps of vast environments, use them to perform map-based navigation, and might even be reusing the same circuitry used in spatial reasoning for creating and using maps of arbitrary task-spaces. In contrast, current embodied AI systems either rely on hand-engineered mapping pipelines, which break in the presence of unmodeled dynamics and are restricted to metric space, or on learned policies that rarely form map-like representations at all. Developing architectures that could learn to build and use map-like representations as flexibly as animals is, however, difficult because few embodied AI benchmarks actually require map-based reasoning. To address this, we present ForagerSim --- an interdisciplinary research platform and simulation environment focused on embodied tasks that require map-based reasoning, with scenarios ranging from mobile-robot search and rescue to animal foraging in both complex mazes and vast, potentially infinite open areas. ForagerSim is highly modular and allows modifying independent axes of difficulty related to perception (abstract 2D sensing to full RGB or LiDAR), scale (room-scale to multi-km scale), topology (open-fields to complex mazes), dynamics (smoke, debris, sensorimotor failures and others) and tasks (from simple 2D coverage to foraging-inspired well-alternation tasks). We compare reinforcement learning baselines with a simple engineered robotics stack and a human player on 8 example worlds which show how different difficulty axes affect existing methods. Our results show that, when sensing is simplified to 2D, learned policies can perform multi-object search and well-alternation tasks surprisingly well in simple topologies, but they fall short of human performance in larger or more complex-topology environments where map-based baselines perform well, suggesting that map-based reasoning is the bottleneck in these scenarios.
authors: Tom\'a\v{s} Musil, Martin Kot\'ik, Michal Vavre\v{c}ka, Karla \v{S}t\v{e}p\'anov\'a, Sebastian Scherer, Martin Saska
bullets: Targets the lack of embodied-AI benchmarks that require flexible, map-like reasoning.
Provides tasks spanning robot search and rescue, animal foraging, coverage, and well alternation.
Varies perception, scale, topology, environmental dynamics, and task difficulty independently.
Compares reinforcement-learning agents, an engineered mapping stack, and human performance across eight worlds.
With simplified 2D sensing, learned policies work in simple settings but lag behind humans and map-based methods in larger or more complex environments.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ForagerSim, a simulation environment designed to evaluate map-based reasoning in embodied agents, covering tasks like mobile-robot search and rescue and foraging, directly addressing a gap in current benchmarks for map-based navigation.
papers.title: ForagerSim: Evaluating Embodied Map-Based Reasoning in Large-Scale Dynamic Worlds
papers.tldr: ForagerSim is a modular benchmark for testing map-based reasoning in embodied agents across large, dynamic environments, revealing that learned policies struggle with scale and complex topology.

papers.abstract: Bringing legacy video back to contemporary screens does not necessarily make it look contemporary. Earlier imaging pipelines often leave color casts, muted chroma, weak con- trast, and tonal imbalance, while correcting these character- istics still relies heavily on expert colorists and scales poorly to long, multi-shot videos. We formulate long video color modernization, a task that updates the chromatic and tonal appearance of legacy color footage while preserving scene content and coherence across frames and shots. We introduce a scalable, training-free framework that jointly modernizes grids of temporally adjacent keyframes using a pretrained text-guided image editing model, producing coherent con- temporary references without paired supervision. Compact shot-specific color transforms then propagate these adjust- ments throughout each shot, preserving spatial structure and temporal stability. We conduct a multidimensional evaluation on diverse legacy videos spanning five decades. We combine a human evaluation of perceived modernness with quantita- tive measures of content fidelity, temporal stability, percep- tual quality, and efficiency, and introduce Source-Weighted Inter-shot Grade Consistency (SW-IGC) to assess grade co- herence across shots. On our evaluation set, our frame- work achieves the highest perceived modernness while re- maining competitive across complementary measures, open- ing a path toward the systematic study of long video color modernization. Code is available at https://github.com/jiwoomood/ Video_Color_Modernization.git
authors: Dongyun Kim, Jiwoo Choi, Jaeseong Lee, Seon Joo Kim
bullets: Targets color casts, muted chroma, weak contrast, and tonal imbalance in legacy footage without relying on expert colorists.
Uses a pretrained text-guided image editor to modernize grids of temporally adjacent keyframes without paired training data.
Propagates keyframe adjustments through each shot with compact, shot-specific color transforms for spatial and temporal stability.
Evaluated diverse legacy videos spanning five decades using human modernness judgments and measures of fidelity, stability, quality, efficiency, and cross-shot consistency.
Achieves the highest perceived modernness while remaining competitive on complementary evaluation measures.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses long video color modernization, focusing on temporal coherence and using tools for video understanding. The method involves semantic temporal decomposition and adaptive tool calling, which are relevant to long-form video understanding.
papers.title: From Legacy to Contemporary: Scalable Color Modernization for Long Video
papers.tldr: A training-free framework modernizes the color and tone of long legacy videos while preserving content and maintaining consistency across frames and shots.

papers.abstract: Every driving scene is logged once, but driving is one-to-many: the scene determines which behaviors are feasible, while an instruction selects among them. A log records only the action taken, leaving no direct supervision for alternative feasible actions or instructions the scene cannot support. Consequently, a policy that ignores language and one that follows it without regard to scene constraints can fit the same data. We present Cartender, which learns from the drives not taken. Counterfactual Branching constructs matched and mismatched instruction-action pairs from real recordings without a simulator: a vision-language model proposes alternative futures and their selecting instructions, while unsupported instructions provide negative labels. A learned scene-language compatibility score regulates language conditioning in trajectory generation, and a reward-trained language residual re-ranks generated candidates over a scene-based score. The branches are used for training; instruction following is evaluated by swapping instructions under identical recorded inputs and measuring behavior rather than agreement with generated targets. On WOD-E2E, the best of four proposals achieves an RFS of 8.642 across 3,603 feasible instruction conditions. Across 8,974 admitted proposals, mean RFS is 8.203 versus 7.906 for matched logged trajectories, and 67% score higher than their logged counterpart. Compared with matched-only imitation using the same backbone, Cartender improves same-scene paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and RFS from 6.32 to 7.10; its gate reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.
authors: Zhiwen Chen, Benjin Zhu, Yan Xie, Jun Ma
bullets: Driving logs show only the action taken, providing no direct supervision for feasible alternatives or infeasible instructions.
Counterfactual Branching uses a vision-language model to generate alternative futures and instructions, with mismatches serving as negative labels without a simulator.
A scene-language compatibility gate regulates language conditioning, while a reward-trained language residual re-ranks trajectory candidates.
On WOD-E2E, Cartender improves paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.
Evaluation swaps instructions on identical recorded inputs and measures behavior, rather than agreement with generated targets.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned driving with counterfactual learning and scene-language compatibility.
papers.title: Cartender: Verifiable Language-Conditioned Driving by Learning the Drives Not Taken
papers.tldr: Cartender enables verifiable language-conditioned driving by learning which alternative instructions and trajectories are feasible—or unsupported—from logged scenes.

papers.abstract: An inference budget is useful only when the system delivers an answer within it. We study a fixed-budget policy combining first-valid-box stopping with a charged finalization cue. On 100 fresh, independently audited GSM8K test questions per model, it improves delivered endpoint accuracy over first-box stopping by 8.0 percentage points for Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and 7.0 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. A prelocked repeat on the same questions gives 7.0 and 10.0 points; neither seed shows a gross harm relative to first-box stopping. The point estimates of incremental physical-slot savings are below one percent. A finalization-only ablation separates cue recovery from stopping, and a fixed scalar reader tests extraction as an alternative explanation. The cue is prior art; the contribution is a component and readout analysis with charged injections and verified paths. Results cover two checkpoints, one task, one prompt family, and two fixed seed conditions.
authors: Yupeng Chang, Linyuan Gao, Zhiyuan Li, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang
bullets: Evaluated on 100 independently audited GSM8K test questions per model using Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B.
Improved endpoint accuracy over first-box stopping by 8.0 and 7.0 percentage points, respectively; a prelocked repeat yielded 7.0 and 10.0 points.
Finalization-only ablations and a fixed scalar reader distinguish cue recovery, stopping, and extraction effects.
Incremental physical-slot savings were below 1%, and no seed showed gross harm relative to first-box stopping.
Scope is limited to two checkpoints, one task, one prompt family, and two fixed seed conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Fixed-budget stopping and finalization policy for LLM answer delivery under shared token budgets.
papers.title: Answer Delivery Under a Shared Token Budget: An Audited Study of Stopping and Finalization
papers.tldr: A charged finalization cue combined with first-valid-box stopping improves delivered GSM8K endpoint accuracy under a shared token budget, though physical-slot savings are negligible.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling can improve LLM reasoning, but existing approaches typically adapt generation or apply answer selection after a predetermined generation schedule. We study within-instance allocation: under a hard per-instance prompt-plus-completion token cap, when should inference stop, generate another candidate, or spend residual tokens adjudicating candidates already observed? BOSS is a training-free policy for this three-way decision, with worst-case budget checks before every generation and judge call. Its key contribution is online generation-adjudication allocation under one shared token ledger. Across two Llama-3.1 models and four reasoning benchmarks, BOSS attains the highest accuracy in 22 of 24 model-task-budget cells under the common hard cap. At Llama-3.1-8B and B=4k, it reaches 60.5 macro-average accuracy versus 58.6 for Adaptive-Consistency, 59.1 for TALE-EP, and 58.9 for fixed-schedule League. On identical Stage-I candidate pools, randomized A/B judging with repeated voting improves plurality from 58.4 to 60.3, with the full BOSS selector reaching 60.5. Approximately matched-cost controls further characterize how the benefit of adjudication changes with available inference budget. Together, these results establish generation-adjudication allocation as a distinct design axis for reasoning under strict per-instance caps.
authors: Yupeng Chang, Yahan Li, Chenlu Guo, Diana Inkpen, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang
bullets: Addresses within-instance inference allocation rather than relying on fixed generation schedules or post-hoc selection.
Uses a training-free policy with worst-case token checks before every generation and judge call.
Maintains one shared token ledger for online generation and adjudication decisions.
Achieves the highest accuracy in 22 of 24 model-task-budget settings across two Llama-3.1 models and four reasoning benchmarks.
At Llama-3.1-8B with a 4k-token cap, BOSS reaches 60.5 macro-average accuracy; its scope is reasoning under hard per-instance token caps.
papers.selection_reason: Token-budgeted online sampling and adjudication for LLM reasoning under hard per-instance caps.
papers.title: BOSS: Token-Budgeted Online Sampling and Selection for LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: BOSS adaptively decides whether to stop, generate another reasoning candidate, or adjudicate existing candidates under a strict per-instance token budget.

papers.abstract: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting (IMTSF) requires capturing temporal dynamics and cross-variable dependencies from sparse, asynchronous observations. Existing methods often rely on learned temporal encoders, coupling historical representation construction with model optimisation and repeatedly processing the same observations. We propose CTLite, a lightweight forecasting framework that decouples historical summarisation from learned prediction. Specifically, a parameter-free continuous-time moment encoder summarises local levels and trends at multiple temporal scales while suppressing poorly supported slope estimates. A compact readout combines damped local extrapolation with a low-rank cross-variable correction that accounts for observation freshness, target availability, and forecast horizon. Since the historical summaries are independent of trainable parameters and forecast queries, they can be reused across optimisation steps and repeated predictions for an unchanged history without altering predictions or parameter gradients. Experiments on four real-world benchmarks show that CTLite achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE among the evaluated methods with only 88-2,537 trainable parameters. Under matched GPU workloads at batch size 32, CTLite reduces inference latency by 18.6-87.3% compared with the latest models, including the cost of historical encoding. Reusing summaries further reduces total runtime by approximately 52% over 16 forecast calls on the same history compared with recomputing the encoder for every call, including the initial encoding cost. The code is at: https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-CTLite.
authors: Shusen Ma, Xudong Zuo, Yangchun Xie, Yun-Bo Zhao
bullets: Targets irregular multivariate time series with sparse, asynchronous observations and cross-variable dependencies.
Uses a parameter-free, multi-scale continuous-time moment encoder to summarize local levels and trends while suppressing unreliable slopes.
Combines damped local extrapolation with a compact low-rank correction for cross-variable effects, observation freshness, target availability, and forecast horizon.
Achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE on four real-world benchmarks using only 88–2,537 trainable parameters.
Reduces inference latency by 18.6–87.3% and cuts runtime by about 52% across 16 repeated forecasts when summaries are reused.
papers.selection_reason: Lightweight forecasting framework with reusable summaries and large inference-latency reductions fits the efficient-AI interest.
papers.title: CTLite: Lightweight Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Reusable Continuous-Time Summaries
papers.tldr: CTLite enables lightweight, efficient forecasting of sparse asynchronous multivariate time series by reusing parameter-free continuous-time historical summaries.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are critical for adapting large models under resource-constrained settings. However, as mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, which offer efficient inference at massive parameter scales, gain increasing prevalence in the community, a critical gap arising from the lack of systematic recipes for applying PEFT to MoE models. To narrow this gap, we conduct a large-scale systematic study that investigates a set of essential design recipes, including which modules should be adapted, which granularity should be used to adapt MoE modules, which PEFT method to use, and to what extent should the load-balancing objective be used, across three MoE backbones on downstream tasks and general knowledge tasks. Our experiments yield several key insights. First, adapting MoE experts alone achieves the highest downstream performance with competitive general capability retention under a comparable parameter budget. Second, native expert-weight updates offer a better downstream--retention trade-off than adapters that bypass experts or entire MoE modules. Third, LoRA and DoRA together define the strongest operating region for high downstream accuracy among the evaluated PEFT methods. Fourth, no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates the zero baseline. We finally evaluate a weight-level redesign of MoE$^2$-LoRA on Qwen3. Moving its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and a 3.2-point average downstream cost.
authors: Minglei Li, Peng Ye, Haonan He, Jingqi Ye, Qingyu Yang, Tao Chen
bullets: Studies PEFT design choices across three MoE backbones, downstream tasks, and general-knowledge tasks.
Adapting experts alone achieves the strongest downstream performance while retaining general capabilities under similar parameter budgets.
Native expert-weight updates provide a better performance–retention trade-off than bypassing experts or whole MoE modules.
LoRA and DoRA form the strongest operating region for downstream accuracy; nonzero load-balancing coefficients do not Pareto-dominate zero.
A redesigned MoE²-LoRA that moves its bypass pool into expert weights improves four upstream endpoints by 2.4–17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Systematic PEFT study for MoE LLMs, directly relevant to LLM architecture and adaptation.
papers.title: An Empirical Study of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that PEFT for MoE LLMs works best when directly adapting native expert weights, especially with LoRA or DoRA, while omitting load-balancing objectives.

papers.abstract: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.
authors: Adri\'an S\'anchez-Freire, Gonzalo P\'erez-G\'omez, Aitziber Atutxa, Ander Barrena
bullets: Expanding retrieval collections can change performance patterns observed on small or controlled corpora.
Abstract retrieval works best for abstract-aligned evidence, while full-text is preferable when richer evidence is needed.
Hierarchical full-text retrieval usually matches or exceeds flat full-text performance while using 67% fewer indexed units and 44–56% less storage.
RAG improved most external benchmark configurations and all held-out test configurations, with gains of up to 9.6 and 30.3 percentage points, respectively.
Reranking benefits depend on the corpus and retrieval setting; design choices should reflect evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates RAG design trade-offs, directly relevant to LLM external memory and retrieval.
papers.title: Large-Scale Biomedical RAG: Corpus Scaling, Document Representation, and Efficiency Trade-offs
papers.tldr: A large-scale biomedical RAG evaluation shows that corpus size, evidence representation, and reranking jointly determine accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can ground LLM outputs in domain-specific knowledge, but legal documents are hard: standard chunking fragments hierarchical argument structure, and generic embeddings struggle with both precise citation matching and semantic understanding. We propose StrucChunk (Structure Aware Chunking) with hybrid dense-sparse retrieval for hierarchically structured legal documents. It treats documents as directed acyclic graphs of provisions, preserves clause boundaries, resolves cross-references before embedding, and combines BM25 with BGE-M3 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. We evaluate on five corpora, three legal traditions and two languages. StrucChunk reaches 100% boundary precision (vs. 7.7% for recursive splitting on CrPC), preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references (vs. 0%), and matches section coverage with 40.3% fewer chunks on GDPR. On LegalBench-RAG (6,858 query-passage pairs), it achieves Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% vs. 23.59% for the best baseline (+104%), surpassing the published state of the art by +83%. On 501 queries each for CrPC and CPC (Indian law), Recall@5 improves from 0.557 to 0.804 (+44.4%) and from 0.158 to 0.259 (+64.6%); chunking accounts for 88% and 73% of the gain. On 501 GDPR queries, Recall@5 is 0.868 with R@1 improving +59%. On NitiBench-CCL (3,730 Thai financial law queries), HR@5 is 0.856 vs. 0.594 for naive chunking (+44.1%), showing that section-boundary alignment is the dominant factor across languages, and cross-reference augmentation adds +2.3% on cross-reference queries. We release the implementation, 5,256 evaluation queries across five legal corpora, annotation methodology and chunking quality metrics. Code: github.com/SinghSuryaDeep/legal-rag-strucchunk-1
authors: Surya Deep Singh, Ashutosh Tripathi, Gaurav Deep Singh
bullets: Represents legal documents as provision graphs, preserves clause boundaries, and resolves cross-references before embedding.
Combines BM25 and BGE-M3 retrieval using Reciprocal Rank Fusion for precise citation and semantic matching.
Achieves perfect boundary precision, preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references, and uses 40.3% fewer chunks while maintaining section coverage on GDPR.
Improves retrieval substantially across benchmarks, including Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% on LegalBench-RAG and higher Recall@5/HR@5 on Indian, European, and Thai legal queries.
Releases implementation, evaluation queries, annotation methodology, and chunking-quality metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Structure-aware chunking improves retrieval for RAG, directly relevant to LLM external memory and memory retrieval.
papers.title: StrucChunk: Structure-Aware Retrieval for Legal Document RAG
papers.tldr: StrucChunk improves legal RAG retrieval by preserving document structure and combining hybrid search, substantially outperforming conventional chunking across five multilingual legal corpora.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through parallel reasoning and asynchronous information gathering. Controlled replay across two model families and three benchmarks shows that delivery timing redirects search decisions made before all results arrive, despite identical initial evidence. Acquisition disagreement reaches up to 24 percentage points above same-order repeat variation. This dependence persists after all initial evidence arrives and through a second search, turning temporary differences in what agents have seen into lasting differences in what they acquire. An acquisition-regret bound with a matching construction shows that invariance at a fixed early arrival count can limit the use of evidence already received. We introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which instead releases local reasoning when each subquestion's evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order. For a fixed plan and stable conditional response law, we prove joint invariance of decisions, acquisitions, and answers. With question-only plans across three benchmarks, CEA brings acquisition disagreement to within 1.0 percentage point of repeat variation and achieves accuracy comparable to complete-input controls, improving over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points. Replacing CEA's fixed allocation with first-ready allocation under contention adds 21.6 percentage points of acquisition disagreement, while local query-target disagreement remains near repeat variation. Timed comparisons show that CEA reaches decisions earlier and responds faster than the same program waiting for all initial evidence.
authors: Ruiyang Ren, Yuhao Wang, Yinan Zhang, Chunyan Miao
bullets: Controlled replays show that arrival timing changes what agents search for, even with identical initial evidence.
These differences persist after all initial results arrive and through subsequent searches.
The paper introduces CEA, which triggers local reasoning only when each subquestion’s evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order.
CEA reduces acquisition disagreement to near repeat variation, matches complete-input accuracy, and improves accuracy over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points.
Under contention, first-ready allocation reintroduces substantial disagreement, whereas CEA makes decisions earlier and responds faster than waiting for all initial evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Studies evidence acquisition and scheduling in language-model agents, relevant to reasoning in language foundation models.
papers.title: The Scheduler Is a Hidden Retriever: How Asynchrony Shapes Evidence Acquisition in Search Agents
papers.tldr: Asynchronous evidence delivery can permanently steer search-agent behavior, while Confluent Evidence Acquisition largely removes this timing dependence without sacrificing accuracy or speed.

papers.abstract: Work on efficient large-language-model inference has concentrated almost entirely on reducing the cost of decoding once a request is complete. The quantity a user experiences, however, is the interval between submitting a request and receiving a usable response, and that interval can be shortened without making decoding itself faster. While a request is being composed it is already partially specified, yet conventional deployments begin no computation until submission. We propose and study streaming generation, a decoding regime in which the model begins producing a response from an incomplete request and revises it as the remaining input arrives, so that only a small residue of the answer remains to be computed once the request is submitted. We evaluate the regime on autoregressive and diffusion language models, characterise the conditions under which it reduces user-visible latency, and analyse the mechanism responsible.
authors: Nikita Dragunov, Matvey Mikhalchuk, Anton Razzhigaev
bullets: Targets user-perceived latency rather than decoding cost alone.
Generates from incomplete requests and updates the response as more input arrives.
Evaluated with both autoregressive and diffusion language models.
Characterizes when the approach reduces latency and analyzes why it works.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes streaming generation to reduce user-visible LLM latency, directly fitting efficient-inference interests.
papers.title: Answering While You Type: Optimizing Time-to-Answer with Streaming Generation
papers.tldr: Streaming generation computes an answer while the user is still typing, then revises it as input arrives to reduce time-to-answer after submission.

papers.abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.
authors: Song-Li Wu, Chubin Zhang, Wenbo Ding, Yansong Tang
bullets: Addresses robotic photography requiring intent understanding, motion planning, and aesthetic image composition.
Uses PhotoCoT for structured camera-action planning within a Vision-Language-Action framework.
Applies Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization to align camera behavior with human preferences.
Introduces OpenPhotography, a dataset of language-guided robotic photography demonstrations for training and evaluation.
Real-world experiments show effective generalization to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex instructions.
papers.selection_reason: VLA framework for autonomous robotic photography with language-guided camera control.
papers.title: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.tldr: RoboPhoto-VLA unifies visual understanding, language reasoning, and camera control to autonomously produce aesthetically preferred photographs across varied real-world scenarios.

papers.abstract: Video-Language Models (VLMs) excel at visual recognition but struggle with causal reasoning. Current evaluations are flawed: multiple-choice QA allows shortcuts, and open-ended QA lacks robust automatic evaluation. We introduce Causal Chain Generation (CCG), a novel task where models have to generate the sequence of intermediate events connecting a cause and an effect. This structured setup demands genuine reasoning and enables reliable automatic scoring. We accompany this task with two complementary metrics: SODA-Embedding, which measures the semantic matching of a generated chain against a reference, and Causal-QA, which probes the chain's causal coherence by asking whether it contains the specific causal facts needed to reconstruct the narrative. We provide two test sets: SF20K-CC, a manually annotated diagnostic on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, a movie clip benchmark derived from audio descriptions. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with narrative causality understanding, frequently hallucinating or omitting key events. To address this, we fine-tune VLMs with GRPO using a composite reward that combines a format reward, SODA-Embedding, and Causal-QA accuracy, demonstrating substantial improvements over strong baselines.
authors: Ridouane Ghermi, Vicky Kalogeiton, Ivan Laptev
bullets: Existing multiple-choice and open-ended evaluations can enable shortcuts or lack reliable automatic scoring for causal reasoning.
Causal Chain Generation (CCG) requires models to produce intermediate events connecting a video’s cause and effect.
SODA-Embedding evaluates semantic similarity to reference chains, while Causal-QA tests whether generated chains contain essential causal facts.
Two benchmarks are presented: SF20K-CC, based on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, derived from movie audio descriptions.
State-of-the-art VLMs often hallucinate or omit key events; GRPO fine-tuning with a composite reward substantially improves performance over strong baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses video-language causal reasoning and VLM fine-tuning, fitting video understanding and multimodal LLM interests.
papers.title: From Cause to Effect: Generating Intermediate Event Chains in Videos
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a structured task and evaluation framework for testing and improving video-language models’ ability to generate causally coherent event chains between causes and effects.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Diffusion Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm for long video generation. However, they are often constrained by prohibitive computational overhead and substantial memory footprints. This inefficiency arises from dense computation mechanisms that allocate uniform processing resources across all spatiotemporal regions, failing to leverage the inherent temporal redundancy of video where motion is typically confined to sparse areas. In this paper, we propose Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA), a unified framework that shifts from dense computation to sparse, motion-driven generation to eliminate both storage and computational redundancies. Inspired by video codec principles, our approach explicitly decouples video content into dynamic and static regions. To mitigate memory bottlenecks, we selectively compress the historical KV cache by retaining only dynamic features within the generated chunk. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we employ a region-level computation allocation strategy based on localized dynamics. Additionally, a dynamics-guided distillation method is introduced to enhance performance via a lightweight distillation training process. Experiments on VBench demonstrate that our approach accelerates autoregressive video generation by 2.16x, while preserving high visual fidelity.
authors: Yuanyu He, Zhuokun Chen, Yefei He, Zhiwei Tang, Jiasheng Tang, Yinghao Yu, Jianfei Cai, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and memory usage of dense autoregressive video diffusion.
Separates dynamic and static regions to exploit temporal redundancy in videos.
Compresses historical KV caches by retaining dynamic features and allocates computation according to localized motion.
Uses dynamics-guided distillation to improve performance with lightweight training.
On VBench, achieves 2.16× faster generation while maintaining high visual fidelity.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets efficient autoregressive video diffusion with sparse attention and KV cache compression, fitting efficient AI and video generation interests.
papers.title: Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: DASA makes autoregressive video diffusion more efficient by focusing computation and memory on regions with motion while preserving visual quality.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.
authors: Marwan Farag, Bin Yang
bullets: Targets the high cost of processing dense, long-form audio token sequences in Large Audio Language Models.
Scores tokens conditioned on the user’s question rather than relying on attention, similarity, or temporal-sampling heuristics.
Distills token rankings from a frozen LALM’s answer-gradient saliency and uses downstream answer supervision.
At 10% token retention, achieves the best or tied-best performance on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks.
Evaluated across speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification, among other tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Question-aware audio token pruning for large audio language models; directly fits token pruning/eviction and multimodal LLM efficiency.
papers.title: AudioScorer: Learning Question-Aware Token Relevance for Large Audio Language Models
papers.tldr: AudioScorer learns question-aware audio-token relevance to reduce LALM processing costs while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: We investigate multi-constraint policy optimization in constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), where interactions among constraint gradients often yield ill-conditioned update directions, causing numerically fragile steps and unintended cancellation or redundant overlap in constraint corrections. To address this, we propose LOCU, which mitigates numerical instability arising from constraint interactions by applying symmetric Lowdin orthogonalization to the natural gradients of the reward and constraints under the Fisher-Rao metric. Combined with Fisher-geometric screening and near-collinear compression, LOCU yields a compact reduced space in which the trust region becomes a Euclidean ball and constraints are handled symmetrically through a low-dimensional active-set solve. For infeasible iterates, LOCU constructs a Pareto-descent direction which preserves the local feasibility of satisfied constraints within the same reduced formulation. Experiments show that LOCU remains stable under high constraint coupling, narrow feasible regions, and infeasible starts, and generalizes across different cost critic architectures.
authors: Joonyoung Lim, Younghwan Yoo
bullets: Targets ill-conditioned, fragile update directions caused by interacting constraint gradients in CMDPs.
Uses symmetric Löwdin orthogonalization under the Fisher–Rao metric, plus gradient screening and near-collinear compression.
Solves a symmetric low-dimensional active-set problem where the trust region becomes a Euclidean ball.
Provides Pareto-descent directions for infeasible iterates while preserving locally satisfied constraints.
Experiments show stability under strong constraint coupling, narrow feasible regions, and infeasible starts across cost critic architectures.
papers.selection_reason: Constrained policy optimization method for CMDPs is directly transferable to safe robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: LOCU: Lowdin-Orthogonalized Constraint Updates for Multi-Constraint Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: LOCU stabilizes multi-constraint policy optimization by orthogonalizing reward and constraint updates in a Fisher-geometric reduced space.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but remain computationally expensive. Sparse attention and temporal caching reduce computation within and across denoising steps, respectively, offering a natural composition. However, predictions produced with sparse attention become sources for temporal reuse, coupling their errors along the sampling trajectory. We observe that improving the accuracy of these sources recovers fidelity without changing the reuse schedule, and that sparsification errors remain directionally aligned across nearby steps, suggesting that correction information can be shared rather than recomputed. These observations motivate RECAP, a training-free method that couples sparse attention with hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction, adaptively coordinated by online error feedback. Cached dense refinement corrects omitted interactions in current sparse estimates, while fresh sparse statistics track input changes and regulate the aging correction. The resulting predictions then renew the sources for whole-step prediction reuse, allowing prediction history to advance between dense refreshes. We evaluate RECAP on multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention methods, caching methods, and their direct compositions. On HunyuanVideo at 720p 5-second generation, RECAP achieves a 3.05x speedup and outperforms all tested direct compositions in both fidelity and inference speed.
authors: Tiange Xu, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of diffusion transformers for high-quality video generation.
Uses training-free reciprocal correction: cached dense refinement fixes sparse-attention omissions, while fresh sparse statistics monitor input changes.
Employs online error feedback to coordinate sparse attention, hierarchical caching, and correction aging without changing the reuse schedule.
Evaluated across multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention, caching, and direct-composition baselines.
On HunyuanVideo at 720p for 5-second videos, reports a 3.05× speedup and better fidelity and speed than tested direct compositions.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient video diffusion via sparse attention and hierarchical caching, fitting both efficient AI and video diffusion interests.
papers.title: RECAP: Reciprocal Sparse Attention and Hierarchical Caching for Efficient Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: RECAP accelerates video diffusion by combining sparse attention and hierarchical caching with reciprocal error correction, achieving faster and higher-fidelity generation than direct combinations of existing methods.

papers.abstract: When a user supplies a document and wants the answer drawn from it, a language model is expected to follow it even when it contradicts its parametric knowledge. Prior work has focused on making the model rely on context by steering activations, contrasting logits during decoding, or instructing it in plain language. We ask whether the document alone, with no instruction written into it and no access to the model at inference time, is enough. We optimize a document suffix by discrete token search, starting from the answer to a single question and extending the objective to a set of passages, to multi-hop questions that follow from the planted fact, and to later turns of a conversation. On counterfactual passages that contradict parametric knowledge of the model, the suffix flips nearly all items the model resists across three instruction-tuned model families, in most settings outperforms the decoding baseline and the strongest instruction we could write, and matches activation steering. Controls show that the suffix largely acts through the passage rather than injecting the answer, and a single suffix per model transfers to unseen passages. Each extended objective carries the effect to its target, so the objective, not only the document, sets how far the effect reaches.
authors: Gia-Bao Dinh Ho, Sekh Mainul Islam, Masahiro Kaneko, Timothy Baldwin, Isabelle Augenstein
bullets: The work studies whether a document alone can override a model’s parametric knowledge.
It uses discrete token search to optimize suffixes for single questions, passage sets, multi-hop reasoning, and later conversation turns.
On counterfactual passages, suffixes flip nearly all resisted items across three instruction-tuned model families.
They usually outperform decoding-based intervention and written instructions, and match activation steering.
Controls suggest the effect mainly operates through the passage; model-specific suffixes also transfer to unseen passages.
papers.selection_reason: Studies optimized suffixes to steer language-model context following, relevant to LLM behavior and instruction-following.
papers.title: Shaping the Document, Not the Model: Optimized Suffixes for Context Following
papers.tldr: Optimized document suffixes can make language models follow contradictory context without modifying the model or adding instructions at inference time.

papers.abstract: Tool-using voice agents often leave users waiting after speech ends, even when actionable information arrives earlier in the request. Speculative approaches begin work during speech, but chunk-bounded or interrupt-on-update generation can truncate a tool call before its arguments are complete. This couples computation time to speech updates, limiting useful work completed in advance. We introduce Heartbeat Thinking, which handles updated input through new Thinker invocations while allowing ongoing invocations and dispatched tools to finish. Periodic invocations read the latest partial transcript and a shared record of completed reasoning and tool results. These results help resolve missing arguments and initiate dependent calls, allowing preparation to progress across speech updates. Across SpeechFCEval, FDBench v3, and AudioCRAG, Heartbeat improves aggregate speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse over a SHANKS-style windowed baseline, with benchmark-dependent effects on final task quality. On FDBench v3, it increases tool coverage by 16 percentage points and reduces mean final-response latency by 36.4\%. The results show that heartbeat thinking paradigm preserving ongoing computation during speech can turn listening time into reusable preparation for faster and more capable voice-agent responses.
authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Kewei Fu, Yongqi Tong, Chenzhi Zheng, Wei Wu, Jiang-Ming Yang, Jianshe Li
bullets: Addresses wasted listening time and truncated tool calls in realtime voice agents.
Starts new Thinker invocations on updated partial transcripts while preserving ongoing reasoning and dispatched tools.
Shares completed reasoning and tool results to fill missing arguments and launch dependent calls.
Across three benchmarks, it improves speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse, with benchmark-dependent effects on final quality.
On FDBench v3, tool coverage rises by 16 percentage points and mean final-response latency falls by 36.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Concerns tool-using LLM voice agents with speculative execution and latency reduction, relevant to LLM deployment and reasoning.
papers.title: Heartbeat Thinking: Speculative Reasoning and Tool Execution While Listening in Realtime Voice Agents
papers.tldr: Heartbeat Thinking lets voice agents continue and reuse speculative reasoning and tool calls across speech updates, reducing post-speech response latency.

papers.abstract: Subword tokenization methods such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) are a core component of modern language models; yet, tokenizer capacity remains typically determined by a fixed merge budget, chosen heuristically. Since larger vocabularies increase memory usage and computational cost, selecting compact and effective token inventories is essential for efficient language modeling. We study the optimization of a BPE merge budget as a statistical model selection problem and investigate information-theoretic criteria for \emph{computing optimal merge sets} directly from corpus statistics. To further improve the merge selection in limited data conditions, we augment the BPE training corpora with synthetic texts generated from the original data, providing estimates for the unigram and bigram distributions. Experiments across multiple corpora and downstream tasks show that using a principled vocabulary selection technique reduces model size, with little degradation in performance. We further observe that synthetic data can yield better tokenizers, especially in low-resource settings.
authors: Vijini Liyanage, Fran\c{c}ois Yvon
bullets: Fixed BPE merge budgets are often chosen heuristically, despite their impact on memory and computation.
The study uses information-theoretic criteria and corpus statistics to compute effective merge sets directly.
Synthetic text augmentation improves unigram and bigram estimates for tokenizer selection in limited-data settings.
Experiments across corpora and downstream tasks find reduced model size with little degradation in performance.
Synthetic data is especially helpful for tokenizer quality in low-resource settings.
papers.selection_reason: The paper addresses the optimization of BPE merge budgets for language models, treating the selection process as a statistical model selection problem to reduce memory and computational cost. This is directly relevant to the architecture and efficiency of Large Language Models.
papers.title: Rethinking BPE: Merge Selection as Model Selection
papers.tldr: BPE merge budgets can be selected as a statistical model-selection problem to build smaller token vocabularies with little performance loss.

papers.abstract: RGBA video generation is essential for creating compositable visual assets in filmmaking, game development, and digital content production. However, generating high-quality RGB appearance alongside temporally coherent transparency remains a significant challenge. Existing text-to-RGBA video methods often entangle RGB and alpha distributions and offer limited control over the precise appearance of a target asset. In addition, incorporating image conditioning typically suffers from the emergence-disappearance effects, which fail existing first-frame or first-and-last-frame conditions due to their fully transparent boundary frames. To address these issues, we present Wan-Alpha++, a unified framework that brings controllable RGBA video generation to both text- and image-to-video diffusion backbones through a shared RGBA latent space, extending our conference version Wan-Alpha from the text-conditioned setting to image-conditioned generation with an interior reference frame. Our method first learns shiftable RGB-alpha distributions while preserving the pretrained RGB prior. Specifically, we introduce a transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion objective to produce distinguishable RGBA latent representations, and a transparency-guided mean sampler that shifts the noise distribution to improve transparency generation and enable spatial controllability. Building upon this RGBA generation prior, we introduce temporal phase reparameterization for image-conditioned effect generation. By cyclically transforming a zero-positive-zero alpha pattern into a positive-zero-positive pattern, it relocates visible content to both temporal boundaries, facilitating effective appearance conditioning with limited RGBA data.
authors: Haotian Dong, Xin Wang, Wenjing Wang, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Yan Tina Luximon, Ping Li, Wanchao Su, Ke Xu, Di Lin
bullets: Targets entangled RGB–alpha generation and weak image-conditioning behavior at transparent video boundaries.
Uses a shared RGBA latent space across text-to-video and image-to-video diffusion backbones.
Introduces transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion and a transparency-guided mean sampler for improved and spatially controllable transparency.
