Applies temporal phase reparameterization to convert zero-positive-zero alpha patterns into boundary-visible positive-zero-positive patterns for image conditioning.
Extends Wan-Alpha from text-conditioned generation to image-conditioned transparent effects using an interior reference frame.
papers.selection_reason: Controllable RGBA video generation built on diffusion backbones.
papers.title: Wan-Alpha++: Animating a Single RGBA Asset into Controllable Transparent Video Effects
papers.tldr: Wan-Alpha++ generates controllable, temporally coherent transparent RGBA videos from text or a single interior reference image.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical world models plan over long horizons by passing predicted states from a coarse model to a lower-level controller. Choosing these states can be expensive: the upper-level planner repeatedly differentiates through candidate macro-action trajectories. We replace this search with a lightweight goal-conditioned network trained through the frozen high-level predictor. The network supplies a conditioning vector, while the predictor generates the next latent waypoint. Training uses hindsight goals and state-prediction losses on offline trajectories, without search-solution targets or macro-action labels. Inference retains an autoregressive high-level rollout, but requires no high-level candidate optimization. We evaluate this approach on the shared-latent HWM checkpoints distributed with H-JEPA, using three backbone seeds and three head initializations per backbone. With a common evaluation protocol, mean success is 70.4% on Cube, 48.7% on Push-T, 100.0% on FourRoom, and 71.1% on Visual AntMaze. The method improves over the corresponding HWM search baseline on three environments and has the same mean on Push-T. Dedicated measurements on an NVIDIA L40S give 1.28-4.39x end-to-end speedups for batched evaluation. Ablations identify state-adaptive conditioning as a consistent contributor, while predictor-mediated subgoals and unrestricted conditions have environment-dependent benefits.
authors: Xiang Kaibo, Liu Qingfeng
bullets: Uses a frozen high-level predictor to generate latent subgoals from learned conditioning vectors.
Trains on offline trajectories with hindsight goals and state-prediction losses, without search targets or macro-action labels.
Maintains autoregressive high-level rollouts while eliminating candidate optimization at inference.
Achieves mean success of 70.4% on Cube, 48.7% on Push-T, 100.0% on FourRoom, and 71.1% on Visual AntMaze.
Delivers 1.28–4.39× end-to-end speedups; state-adaptive conditioning consistently helps, while other components vary by environment.
papers.selection_reason: Uses frozen hierarchical world models for goal-conditioned subgoal learning and planning.
papers.title: Learning Goal-Conditioned Subgoals through Frozen Hierarchical World Models
papers.tldr: A lightweight goal-conditioned network replaces costly high-level trajectory search in hierarchical world models while preserving strong performance and improving inference speed.

papers.abstract: Tactile perception is crucial for precise robotic manipulation, providing an important foundation for dexterous, closed-loop force control. Among various tactile sensing techniques, magnetic tactile sensors stand out thanks to their fine-grained, three-dimensional force perception capability and strong robustness against visual occlusion. In this study, we discover a physical loophole called PhantomTac in magnetic tactile sensors. The attacker can alter the magnetic field, thus spoofing the force interpreted by magnetic tactile sensors. The attacker can stealthily deploy such an attack by simply attaching a thin (the thickness is around 0.5 mm), battery-free magnetic tag to the surface of an object. Hence, the attack tag can be easily concealed by a barcode sticker. Such an attack scheme is "deploy-and-forget" -- the attacker can deploy the tag and leave. When a robotic hand is picking up an object, it may severely damage the object. Specifically, spoofing the normal force can crush the object, whereas spoofing the shear force can lead to a loose grip, thus dropping the object. Compared with directly sabotaging the robotic hand, PhantomTac is much more concealed as the attacker does not need access to the device. We performed extensive reverse-engineering efforts to characterize the sensing mechanism of commercial-off-the-shelf tactile sensors and proposed a practical tag design. End-to-end evaluations conducted on real robots and robotic arms demonstrate that our attack can bypass existing anti-interference mechanisms and effectively hijack their closed-loop control processes, achieving an attack success rate exceeding 95% when the grasping-position offset is bounded within 8 mm. Finally, based on the limitations of existing anti-magnetic interference mechanisms, we propose a multimodal-consistency defense mechanism to mitigate such physical-layer security threats.
authors: Binbin Zhang, Yifeng Zhang, Xiaomeng Chen, Dongyao Chen
bullets: Targets magnetic tactile sensors by altering their perceived normal and shear forces.
Uses a thin, deploy-and-forget tag that can be concealed under a barcode sticker, without accessing the robot.
Reverse-engineers commercial tactile sensors to develop a practical attack-tag design.
Real-robot evaluations show the attack can bypass existing defenses and achieve over 95% success when grasping-position offset is within 8 mm.
Proposes multimodal consistency checking as a defense against this physical-layer threat.
papers.selection_reason: Physical-layer attack on magnetic tactile sensors in robotic manipulation; relevant to embodied AI perception robustness and closed-loop control security, though not a learning method.
papers.title: PhantomTac: Hijacking Robotic Tactile Systems with Deploy-and-forget Tags
papers.tldr: PhantomTac is a concealed, battery-free magnetic-tag attack that spoofs robotic tactile sensors and hijacks grasping control, potentially crushing or dropping objects.

papers.abstract: Learning from Demonstration (LfD) allows robots to learn new skills from human examples; however, many vision-based methods require large datasets and resource-intensive end-to-end training. This paper introduces a data-efficient LfD framework for humanoid robots that learns manipulation skills from compact, task-specific features instead of raw images. The proposed approach integrates layered visual preprocessing, Kinect-based human joint estimation, prompt-based object detection, and depth information to extract human motion features and three-dimensional object locations from demonstration videos. These features are used to train a temporal deep learning model that predicts robot joint-angle trajectories for execution. The framework is implemented on a NAO humanoid robot, evaluated quantitatively in simulation, and demonstrated on physical hardware. In simulation, the robot achieves a 78% success rate on a pick-and-place task using only 16 demonstrations, which increases to 86% when trained with 100 demonstrations. The framework also achieves a 71% success rate on a pushing task using eight demonstrations, highlighting its effectiveness for data-efficient humanoid skill acquisition.
authors: Keyhan Rayati, AliReza Beigy, Anoosheh Saadati, Pourya Shahverdi, Mehdi Tale Masouleh, Ahmad Kalhor, Wing-Yue Geoffrey Louie
bullets: Addresses the data and compute demands of vision-based Learning from Demonstration.
Extracts human motion and 3D object-location features using layered vision, Kinect joint estimation, prompt-based object detection, and depth.
Trains a temporal deep learning model to predict robot joint-angle trajectories.
Implemented on a NAO robot, with evaluation in simulation and demonstration on physical hardware.
Achieves 78% pick-and-place success with 16 demonstrations, rising to 86% with 100; pushing reaches 71% with eight demonstrations.
papers.selection_reason: Data-efficient LfD from human demonstration videos for humanoid manipulation.
papers.title: Data-Efficient Learning from Demonstration for Humanoid Robots via Feature-Level Perception and Prompt-Based Object Detection
papers.tldr: A feature-based, prompt-assisted vision framework enables humanoid robots to learn manipulation skills from relatively few demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Humanoid manipulation requires reusable arm skills, yet demonstrating every possible skill combination is impractical. We present Humanoid Semantic Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Policy (HS-MoDP), which composes separately demonstrated arm skills through independent semantic routing over a shared expert pool. This design preserves arm-specific skill control while sharing action-generation parameters across arms. A semantic scheduler integrates the learned policy with an existing locomotion controller through alternating manipulation and repositioning stages, extending the effective workspace and enabling skill reuse across location changes. To acquire demonstrations of whole-body contact manipulation, we develop G1Exo, an isomorphic exoskeleton that provides direct joint-level control of arm configurations. Experiments on a Unitree G1 show stronger skill composition than the baselines. G1Exo enables more reliable contact teleoperation than end-effector VR-IK, and its demonstrations improve contact-skill learning across four policy architectures. For HS-MoDP, switching from VR-IK to G1Exo demonstrations raises full cabinet workflow success from 35% to 65%. All project hardware designs and source code will be released as open source after the review process.
authors: Yiming Wang, Peixian Yang, Lifeng Zhuo, Lai Wei, Xinling Du, Kun Song, Weiming Wang, Daolin Ma
bullets: Targets the impracticality of demonstrating every possible combination of humanoid manipulation skills.
HS-MoDP independently routes semantic arm skills through a shared expert pool, preserving arm-specific control while sharing action-generation parameters.
A semantic scheduler alternates manipulation and repositioning with a locomotion controller to extend workspace and reuse skills across locations.
G1Exo enables more reliable contact teleoperation than end-effector VR-IK, improving contact-skill learning across four policy architectures.
On a Unitree G1, G1Exo demonstrations increased full cabinet workflow success from 35% to 65% for HS-MoDP over VR-IK demonstrations.
papers.selection_reason: Compositional humanoid manipulation via diffusion policy and skill routing.
papers.title: Compositional Humanoid Manipulation through Isomorphic Teleoperation and Independent Skill Routing
papers.tldr: HS-MoDP composes reusable humanoid arm skills via semantic expert routing, while G1Exo provides reliable joint-level teleoperation for collecting contact-rich demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Voice-based public services have evolved from manual switchboards to intelligent platforms to meet modern user needs. However, current systems remain constrained by rigid menu-driven interaction, fragmented vertical services, and limited extensibility. To address these issues, we present VISAGENT, an agent-based end-to-end voice interaction system for large-scale public services that integrates end-to-end speech interaction, hierarchical agent routing, a scalable voice-agent marketplace, and user memory support. The system replaces menu-driven workflows with natural speech and dynamically dispatches user requests to either a general conversational model or specialized domain agents via a two-level routing paradigm that achieves sub-second intent-to-agent selection over hundreds of agents. User memory informs preference-aware agent selection and supplies relevant preferences and context to selected agents, supporting personalized task execution and reducing the need for users to repeat previously provided information. A voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational entities, enabling dynamic onboarding and ecosystem-level extensibility. We validate VISAGENT through a real-world deployment in China's 114 hotline across multiple service domains. Experimental results demonstrate low-latency full-duplex interaction, robust routing scalability, and competitive speech naturalness. More broadly, this work advocates a shift from isolated voice assistants toward agent-centric conversational infrastructures, providing a general blueprint for building extensible voice-agent systems in public services and beyond.
authors: Xiang Wang, Zhaoxiang Liu, Xiang Chen, Liqiang He, Kai Wang, Shiguo Lian
bullets: Targets rigid menu systems, fragmented services, and limited extensibility in public-service voice platforms.
Combines end-to-end speech interaction, two-level hierarchical routing, a voice-agent marketplace, and user memory.
Routes requests to general or specialized agents and uses stored preferences and context for personalized task execution.
Supports dynamic onboarding of task agents as conversational entities, enabling ecosystem-level extensibility.
Validated in China’s 114 hotline, demonstrating low-latency full-duplex interaction, scalable routing, and competitive speech naturalness.
papers.selection_reason: Agent-based voice interaction system with user memory and routing, relevant to agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: VISAGENT: An Agent-Based End-to-End Voice Interaction System
papers.tldr: VISAGENT is an extensible, agent-based voice interaction platform that replaces rigid public-service menus with natural conversation, scalable routing, and personalized agent support.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion has emerged as a leading paradigm for efficient video generation, yet its practical deployment remains bottlenecked by the trade-off between generation quality and inference efficiency. We attribute this bottleneck to three error sources in AR rollouts: the base model error, the train-inference distribution mismatch, and the upstream error propagation. Building on this decomposition, we derive closed-form upper bounds on the per-step and cumulative errors, providing a principled basis for jointly optimizing generation quality and inference efficiency. Guided by this analysis, we propose TriTD, a Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution co-optimized distillation framework with three complementary modules. First, for ODE initialization, we adopt a Next-Node Trajectory Distillation (NTD) objective, which shortens the supervision horizon and admits a lower regression-error floor. Second, we introduce Chunk-Graded Noising (CGN), a monotonically non-decreasing per-chunk noising schedule that helps narrow the expected train-inference noise mismatch and removes redundant KV-cache updates, yielding substantial speedups at no quality cost. Third, we propose Orthogonal-Parallel DMD (OP-DMD), a distribution-matching loss that retains the original DMD supervision while introducing an additional regression constraint in the orthogonal subspace to suppress off-axis drift, improving both training stability and final generation quality. Extensive experiments show that TriTD consistently surpasses existing baselines in visual quality while reaching a real-time throughput of 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU, delivering a balanced quality-efficiency solution for interactive streaming video generation.
authors: Jia Li, Xurui Peng, Haowei Zhu, Tianyu Zhao, Jiexi Wang, Youwei Zheng, Yuxi Ren, Xinglong Wu, Xing Wang, Hayden Kwok-Hay So
bullets: Targets three AR rollout issues: base-model error, train–inference distribution mismatch, and upstream error propagation.
Derives closed-form bounds for per-step and cumulative errors to guide quality–efficiency optimization.
Combines Next-Node Trajectory Distillation, Chunk-Graded Noising, and Orthogonal-Parallel DMD.
Chunk-Graded Noising reduces redundant KV-cache updates without sacrificing quality, while OP-DMD improves stability and generation quality.
Experiments report consistent visual-quality gains over existing baselines and real-time throughput for interactive streaming video generation.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive video generation distillation with KV-cache efficiency improvements.
papers.title: TriTD: Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution Distillation for Real-Time Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: TriTD improves autoregressive video diffusion by jointly reducing rollout errors, enabling higher visual quality and real-time generation at 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

papers.abstract: While language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their performance remains disproportionately skewed towards high-resource languages. This disparity is particularly acute for the 700 million inhabitants of Southeast Asia, where vast linguistic diversity remains under-represented in existing benchmarks, often suffering from limited language coverage or narrow task scopes. To address this, we introduce DeepSEA, a comprehensive benchmark constructed from established datasets through professional human translation into 12 Southeast Asian languages, spanning both high-resource (e.g., Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese) and low-resource (e.g., Burmese, Khmer, Lao) tiers across five distinct tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation. Extensive evaluation of frontier proprietary and open-weights models reveals that while frontier models like Gemini-3.7-Flash maintain robustness across resource tiers, smaller models face severe performance degradation on low-resource languages. Crucially, models perform better in reasoning and summarization when pivoted through English rather than target languages, exposing a critical dependency on English representations, especially for low-resource languages. Beyond these observations, we provide a cross-lingual error analysis and a cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis. We hope these findings shed light on the development of next-generation inclusive multilingual models.
authors: Jiuzhou Han, Abhishek Bijay Mishra, Trevor Cohn, Shubham Mittal
bullets: Covers five tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation.
Includes professionally translated data across high-resource and low-resource Southeast Asian languages, including Burmese, Khmer, and Lao.
Frontier models are relatively robust across language-resource tiers, while smaller models degrade sharply on low-resource languages.
Reasoning and summarization improve when models pivot through English rather than using target languages directly.
Provides cross-lingual error analysis and cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis to diagnose multilingual limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Multilingual evaluation benchmark for Southeast Asian languages, relevant to LLM evaluation and multilingual capabilities.
papers.title: DeepSEA: A Multilingual Evaluation Benchmark for Southeast Asia
papers.tldr: DeepSEA benchmarks multilingual model performance across 12 Southeast Asian languages and shows that low-resource languages remain especially challenging, with models often relying on English for reasoning and summarization.

papers.abstract: Multi-label classification is particularly challenging in streaming scenarios, where data arrives sequentially. Online kernel methods offer a promising solution. However, prevailing methods rely on a single preselected kernel, making them prone to suboptimal choices since the global data distribution is unknown in advance in online settings. Although the recent method, Online Kernel Selection for Online Multi-label Classification (OKS-OMC), enables data-driven kernel selection, it fails to fully harness the complementary information from multiple kernels and encounters the curse of kernelization. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel online multi-kernel combination method for large-scale multi-label classification. First, an efficient and robust online single-kernel multi-label method is designed. Second, learning an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers is formalized as a structural risk minimization problem. An improved alternating optimization procedure is developed, in which the combination coefficients are updated by directly minimizing the objective function, while each kernel classifier is updated by minimizing a surrogate upper bound. This procedure decouples the learning of kernel classifiers from combination coefficients, allowing independent classifier updates via our single-kernel method and accelerating convergence to high-quality solutions. Our multi-kernel method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best fixed single-kernel models chosen in hindsight. Ablation studies confirm that our method's components outperform their counterparts in OKS-OMC. Comprehensive evaluations across 11 datasets and seven metrics demonstrate our method's overall superiority over existing online multi-label methods.
authors: Tingting Zhai, Wei Liu, Renjian Yu
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of choosing kernels when the data distribution is unknown in advance.
Learns an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers through structural risk minimization.
Uses alternating optimization: combination coefficients directly minimize the objective, while classifiers minimize surrogate upper bounds.
The method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best hindsight-selected single-kernel models.
Ablations and evaluations on 11 datasets using seven metrics show improvements over OKS-OMC and other online multi-label methods.
papers.selection_reason: Online multi-kernel combination for streaming multi-label classification; fits online learning.
papers.title: Optimal Multi-Kernel Combination for Online Multi-Label Classification
papers.tldr: An online multi-kernel method improves streaming multi-label classification by learning complementary kernel combinations rather than relying on a single preselected kernel.

papers.abstract: We present PnP-Transformer, a neural pose solver designed as an iterative-free, differentiable alternative to classical PnP-RANSAC algorithms. PnP-Transformer regresses the 6D object pose by processing predicted semi-dense 2D-3D correspondence fields alongside confidence scores, while mapping geometric inputs into a continuous latent space. To evaluate its practical utility, we integrate PnP-Transformer into a zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipeline, where the correspondence module and pose solver are trained separately. PnP-Transformer achieves a 41.2% mean AR score with low latency (0.46 s/obj) on seven core BOP benchmark datasets, surpassing all prior baselines (such as RayPose with 39.1% AR) but one (Co-op with 58.4% AR). When the pose solver is replaced with EPnP-RANSAC (similar to Co-op) while keeping the correspondence module unchanged, the RANSAC alternative outperforms PnP-Transformer on six of the seven datasets by reaching 52.2% mean AR at a cost of an additional 60 ms per object, revealing an accuracy-latency trade-off. Code and pretrained models are available: https://github.com/ebylmz/pnp-transformer
authors: Emirkan Burak Yilmaz, Yakup Genc
bullets: Processes semi-dense 2D–3D correspondence fields and confidence scores in a continuous latent space.
Regresses 6D pose without iterative optimization and can be integrated into a zero-shot pipeline with separately trained components.
Achieves 41.2% mean AR at 0.46 s/object across seven core BOP datasets, outperforming most prior baselines but not Co-op.
EPnP-RANSAC reaches 52.2% mean AR with the same correspondence module, at an additional 60 ms/object cost.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Neural 6D object pose estimation is a core 3D vision task.
papers.title: PnP-Transformer: A Neural Pose Solver for 6D Object Pose Estimation
papers.tldr: PnP-Transformer is a fast, differentiable neural alternative to PnP-RANSAC for 6D object pose estimation, but trades some accuracy for lower latency.

papers.abstract: Despite achieving high visual fidelity, video models still suffer from physical hallucinations, limiting their reliability as world simulators. Existing methods leverage model-internal or external signals to improve physical plausibility, but their roles and limitations require a unified explanation. We propose a two-dimensional physical-hallucination risk framework that defines low-density sampling risk and high-density drifting risk. The first risk captures generations assigned low likelihood by the video model, for example, a ball suddenly teleporting despite the model favoring continuous motion, while the second risk captures physical inconsistencies in high-likelihood generations, for example, a ball bouncing progressively higher without additional energy. Our analysis explains how model-internal signals steer sampling toward higher-density regions of the learned distribution to address low-density sampling risk. However, higher model likelihood does not guarantee physical plausibility, motivating external guidance to address high-density drifting risk. Based on this framework, we develop Hallucination-Aware Sampler (HA-Sampler), which applies external physical guidance within latent refinement to generate physically plausible videos, and HA-Scorer, which derives a likelihood-based signal from the generator itself for evaluating generated videos using continuous normalizing flow (CNF), with coarse ODE integration and finite-difference divergence estimates. Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy benchmarks support our theoretical analysis and demonstrate that our methods outperform the compared sampling and scoring SOTA baselines.
authors: Chenyan Zheng, Fan Wu, Ruibo Li, Jiaxing Li, Minghao Yang, Bang Zhang, Guosheng Lin
bullets: Defines low-density sampling risk as unlikely events and high-density drifting risk as physically inconsistent but likely generations.
Explains that model-internal likelihood signals can reduce low-density errors but cannot ensure physical plausibility.
Introduces HA-Sampler, which applies external physical guidance during latent refinement.
Introduces HA-Scorer, a generator-based likelihood signal using continuous normalizing flows for video evaluation.
Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy support the analysis and report better performance than compared SOTA baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Hallucination-Aware Sampler (HA-Sampler) to address physical hallucinations in video generation. Relevant to video world models and video diffusion.
papers.title: Risk Decomposition for Hallucination-Aware Video Sampling
papers.tldr: The paper decomposes physical hallucinations in video generation into low-density sampling errors and high-density physical drift, then introduces tools to mitigate and evaluate both.

papers.abstract: Generalizing real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and spatial discretizations remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce PhysSkin++, a physics-informed framework that learns continuous neural skinning fields from static geometries to construct compact deformation subspaces. Specifically, we propose a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder that predicts shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object network training. To learn these subspaces without simulation trajectories, we develop a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning strategy that combines skinning-field normalization with conflict-aware gradient correction, stabilizing joint optimization under physical and orthogonality constraints. The learned representation supports efficient reduced dynamics with user control and contact interactions, together with direct animation binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians. For prescribed rig animation, we further introduce a self-supervised complementarity objective to learn complementary elastic responses without enforcing complementarity constraints at runtime. Experiments demonstrate cross-shape generalization of the learned skinning fields, real-time reduced simulation, and applications to controllable, collision-aware, and rig-complementary animation.
authors: Yuanhang Lei, Baofei Liu, Xingxuan Li, Tao Cheng, Zixuan Wang, Boming Zhao, Yujun Shen, Siyuan Huang, Ruizhen Hu, Peter Yichen Chen, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of generalizing real-time physics-based animation across shapes and spatial discretizations.
Uses a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder to predict shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object training.
Introduces self-supervised physics-informed learning with normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction, avoiding simulation trajectories.
Supports reduced dynamics with user control, contact interactions, and direct binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians.
Also learns complementary elastic responses for prescribed rig animation; experiments show cross-shape generalization and real-time simulation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PhysSkin++, a framework for physics-based animation via self-supervised neural skinning. Relevant to world models (physics simulation) and 3D vision.
papers.title: PhysSkin++: Real-Time and Generalizable Physics-Based Animation via Self-Supervised Neural Skinning
papers.tldr: PhysSkin++ learns compact, physics-aware deformation subspaces from static shapes, enabling real-time, generalizable animation across diverse 3D representations and interactions.

papers.abstract: Automated treatment planning (ATP) aims to reduce the unwarranted inter-planner variability of manual planning, while improving treatment quality and efficiency. Most ATP pipelines rely on the prediction of the achievable three-dimensional dose distribution for a given anatomy and the subsequent optimization of machine parameters to reproduce it. Diffusion-based methods are largely slice-wise due to the high dimensionality of radiotherapy data, and assume a one-to-one mapping between anatomy and optimal dose despite the multi-objective nature of treatment planning. They are evaluated on their ability to match reference doses and rarely on their integration in ATP frameworks. We present LaDose, a latent diffusion framework for fully volumetric dose prediction. An autoencoder learned on dose distributions, trained so that perturbed latents decode to plausible doses, compresses dose maps 128-fold and enables 3D diffusion on a single GPU. Prescription values are represented as exact scalar vectors that bypass the image encoder, avoiding resampling and latent compression. Multiscale classifier-free guidance allows for the modulation of clinical trade-offs at inference, without retraining or additional labeled data. On 900 clinically delivered head-and-neck volumetric modulated arc therapy plans from five centers, LaDose reached a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy (1.4--1.8\% of the prescription) and was the only one of six frameworks free of systematic bias with respect to the reference distribution. Guidance scales acted predictably on target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing. Integrated with direct aperture optimization, the pipeline generated plans in 15.2 minutes; in a blinded review, senior clinicians rated 14 of 15 plans acceptable without editing.
authors: J. Boyer-Chammard, R. Vauclin, M. C. Biston, P. Maury, M. Gau, S. Stathakis, V. Gr\'egoire, N. Paragios, E. Deutsch, N. Komodakis
bullets: Addresses slice-wise prediction, one-to-one anatomy–dose assumptions, and limited evaluation within complete ATP workflows.
Compresses volumetric dose maps with an autoencoder, enabling 3D diffusion on a single GPU while preserving prescription values as exact scalar inputs.
Uses multiscale classifier-free guidance to adjust target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing without retraining or additional labeled data.
Evaluated on 900 head-and-neck VMAT plans from five centers, achieving a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy and no systematic reference-dose bias among six frameworks.
With direct aperture optimization, plans were generated in 15.2 minutes and 14 of 15 were judged acceptable without editing by senior clinicians.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes LaDose, a latent diffusion framework for volumetric dose prediction in radiotherapy. Relevant to world models (predicting physical manifolds) and 3D vision.
papers.title: Learning the Dose Manifold: A Latent Diffusion Framework for Volumetric Dose Prediction in Automated Radiotherapy Treatment Planning
papers.tldr: LaDose uses latent 3D diffusion to predict clinically controllable radiotherapy dose distributions and integrate them into automated treatment planning.

papers.abstract: External skills provide language-model agents with reusable procedural knowledge, yet how models use such knowledge after it is supplied remains poorly understood. We identify Procedural Exposure Bias (PEB), the tendency of language models to increasingly favor an action as its associated procedural pattern is repeatedly exposed in a skill, even when the interaction state and action relevance remain unchanged. We find that PEB strongly depends on how procedural knowledge is represented: presenting the same content visually substantially attenuates exposure-induced shifts in action preference relative to textual presentation. Further analysis shows that this attenuation primarily arises from visual encoding rather than structured layout. Although repeated procedural signals remain recoverable from Visual representations, they exert a weaker influence on downstream action prediction, distinguishing signal accessibility from its use as action evidence. This effect also extends to executable action selection, where increasing exposure more strongly favors the corresponding action under Text than Visual. Layer-wise analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence becomes more pronounced toward the model output, with stronger evidence under Text, while activation interventions reveal architecture-specific roles of internal components in transmitting or counteracting the preference shift. Complete-agent evaluations across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop further show that Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all four evaluated models. These findings establish skill representation as an important factor governing how procedural knowledge is translated into agent decisions. All code is available at https://github.com/NEUIR/Vis-Skill.
authors: Qing Yang, Yuqi Xiong, Pengcheng Huang, Zhipeng Xu, Zhenghao Liu, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu
bullets: Identifies Procedural Exposure Bias (PEB): repeated procedural patterns increasingly influence action preferences even when state and relevance are unchanged.
The bias is much stronger with textual than visual skill representations; visual encoding, rather than structured layout alone, drives the attenuation.
Visual representations preserve recoverable procedural signals but reduce their use as evidence for downstream action prediction.
Layer-wise and activation analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence grows toward model output and involves architecture-specific components.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all evaluated models.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates Procedural Exposure Bias in skill-augmented language model agents operating in embodied environments (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld). Relevant to both embodied AI and LLMs.
papers.title: Procedural Exposure Bias in Skill-Augmented Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: Repeated textual exposure to procedural skills can bias language-model agents toward associated actions, while visual representations substantially reduce this effect and improve task success.

papers.abstract: Dense temporal audio-visual captioning is important for multimodal video understanding and generation. However, prior work is constrained by three main limitations: (1) the lack of a dataset combining high temporal resolution, longer videos, and bidirectional alignment between time and events; (2) the reliance of most existing RL methods on checklists; and (3) the lack of a benchmark that bidirectionally evaluates event semantic correctness and temporal accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose: (1) AVTime-50K, a high-quality 50K-scale dataset with temporally precise, semantically accurate captions and longer videos; (2) AVTime, a state-of-the-art model optimized with a novel Bidirectional Temporal-Semantic Alignment (BiTSA) reward that imposes explicit bidirectional constraints between time and events; and (3) AVTime-Bench, a specialized benchmark that introduces a novel bidirectional evaluation of temporal accuracy and semantic correctness. Our code, models, and datasets are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Apryle/avtime.
authors: Mingyang Wu, Kaituo Feng, Bohao Li, Kaixiong Gong, Zihao Yin, Xiangyu Yue
bullets: Addresses limitations in temporal resolution, video length, bidirectional time–event alignment, and checklist-based reinforcement learning.
Introduces AVTime-50K, a 50K-scale dataset containing longer videos with temporally precise and semantically accurate captions.
Proposes the Bidirectional Temporal-Semantic Alignment (BiTSA) reward to explicitly constrain alignment between event timing and semantics.
Introduces AVTime-Bench for joint evaluation of temporal accuracy and semantic correctness.
Code, models, and datasets are publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes AVTime dataset and model for dense audio-visual captioning with bidirectional temporal-semantic alignment. Relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: AVTime: Reinforcing Dense Audio-Visual Captions with Bidirectional Alignment
papers.tldr: AVTime advances dense audio-visual video captioning with a large temporally precise dataset, bidirectional reward optimization, and a matching evaluation benchmark.

papers.abstract: Physical interaction is a key capability for humanoid collaboration, requiring coordinated whole-body motion and precise contact. However, learning diverse dual-humanoid interactions faces two major challenges: (1) human-robot morphological differences disrupt contact interfaces and spatial relationships during retargeting, and (2) jointly learning motor skills and partner coordination makes it difficult to retain control fidelity as interaction diversity grows. In this paper, we propose OmniInteract to address these challenges through surface-aware modeling and scalable residual policy learning. First, we introduce Surface Contact-Aware Retargeting, which leverages dense human-robot surface correspondences to jointly retarget both humanoids, preserving explicit interaction contact interfaces and their near-field geometric context. Second, we propose a Scalable Flow-based Interaction Policy for partner-conditioned residual generation. It factorizes dual-humanoid control into a reusable motor foundation and interaction-specific adaptations: partner-aware experts learn corrections over a frozen whole-body motion prior, while conditional flow matching unifies them in a shared residual action space. This enables scalable skill consolidation while retaining pretrained motor capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniInteract improves retargeting fidelity and dual-humanoid coordination while better retaining interaction performance as skill diversity grows. Real-world deployment further demonstrates successful contact establishment, stable whole-body coordination, and recovery from external perturbations.
authors: Yinghao Li, Tianyu Zhang, Zhuohao Li, Yi-Lin Wei, Fa-Ting Hong, Qing Zhang, Wei-Shi Zheng
bullets: Addresses contact and coordination challenges caused by human–robot morphological differences and growing interaction diversity.
Uses dense surface correspondences to jointly retarget both humanoids while preserving contact interfaces and nearby geometry.
Combines a frozen whole-body motion prior with partner-aware residual experts and conditional flow matching.
Experiments show improved retargeting fidelity, coordination, and retention of performance as skills scale.
Real-world tests demonstrate contact establishment, stable coordination, and recovery from external perturbations.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based whole-body interaction control for dual humanoids with residual policies and retargeting.
papers.title: OmniInteract: Towards Unified Whole-Body Interaction Control for Dual Humanoids
papers.tldr: OmniInteract enables diverse dual-humanoid physical interactions through surface-aware retargeting and scalable residual policy learning.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models enable parallel token generation, offering a promising alternative to sequential autoregressive decoding. Existing acceleration methods use predictive confidence to enable parallel token commitment while preserving generation quality. However, confidence-based selection prioritizes reliable token predictions without explicitly considering how token positions shape the remaining decoding schedule. Moreover, such ordering does not always reflect inter-token dependencies, suggesting that confidence need not be the sole criterion for token selection. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding (BPD), which favors central pivots within contiguous masked intervals and decodes the selected positions in parallel. Balanced pivots yield logarithmic decoding depth in the interval length. Our practical method accounts for model uncertainty by combining confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection. We evaluate the resulting quality-efficiency tradeoff on LLaDA and Dream across five mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DLM_random_pivot-EE62/
authors: Yejin Lee, Hyundong Jin, Yo-Sub Han
bullets: Confidence-only decoding overlooks the structure of remaining masked intervals and token dependencies.
BPD selects central pivots within contiguous masked spans, decoding selected positions in parallel.
Balanced pivoting provides logarithmic decoding depth with respect to interval length.
The practical strategy combines confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection.
Evaluated on LLaDA and Dream across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Balance-aware pivot selection for parallel diffusion LLM decoding, improving efficiency via token selection.
papers.title: Balance-Aware Pivot Selection for Parallel Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding accelerates diffusion LLM generation by combining confidence with center-focused parallel token selection to reduce decoding depth.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, although this may weaken the benefit of looping. To study this tradeoff systematically, we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.
authors: Xuyuan Xiong, Siyu Chen, Zihan Shao, Yue Su, Weiyang Jin, Ping Luo, Zhuoran Yang, Xihui Liu
bullets: Looped transformers reuse a shared layer block to add depth without adding trainable parameters.
The study varies model size, training tokens, and forward/backward loop counts across nearly 600 runs.
A unified scaling law models looping and truncation using effective parameters.
When compute is matched, full BPTT with fewer loops consistently beats truncated BPTT.
With model size optimized, two fully trained loops achieve lower loss than a compute-optimal non-looped model using about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and 8% more training compute.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling study of looped transformers with truncated backpropagation; relevant to LLM architecture advances and training-efficiency tradeoffs.
papers.title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
papers.tldr: A large scaling study finds that full backpropagation through looped transformers is generally better than truncated training, with two fully trained loops offering an efficient tradeoff.

papers.abstract: We study regret minimization in finite-horizon episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). While minimax-optimal algorithms are known, tractable approaches to instance-dependent optimality are still lacking. Motivated by this gap, we introduce $\pi_0$-PSRL, a variant of PSRL that uses posterior samples to decide when exploration is needed, while following a fixed reference policy $\pi_0$ during exploration episodes. This decouples the test for exploration, triggered when the sampled and empirical MDPs have different optimal policies, from the choice of the policy used to gather information. The resulting design addresses a limitation of standard PSRL, where the sampled optimal policy may not be the optimal choice for exploration. We prove instance-dependent regret bounds for $\pi_0$-PSRL, identifying the logarithmic exploration cost induced by $\pi_0$ and taking a step toward matching asymptotic lower bounds for episodic RL. Our proof techniques showcase a novel proof structure to derive problem-dependent regret bounds in episodic MDPs, and concentration results for Dirichlet random variables, that may be of independent interest.
authors: Victor Boone, Cyrille Kone, Waris Radji, Odalric-Ambrym Maillard, Dorian Baudry
bullets: Addresses the gap between known minimax-optimal methods and tractable instance-dependent optimality.
Uses posterior samples to trigger exploration when sampled and empirical MDPs have different optimal policies.
Follows a fixed reference policy π₀ during exploration, avoiding potentially poor exploration choices from sampled optimal policies.
Proves instance-dependent regret bounds that characterize the logarithmic exploration cost of π₀.
Introduces proof techniques involving problem-dependent regret analysis and Dirichlet concentration.
papers.selection_reason: Instance-dependent regret bounds for posterior-sampling RL in episodic MDPs; core reinforcement learning method transferable to robot learning.
papers.title: Towards instance-dependent regret optimality in Episodic MDPs with Posterior Sampling
papers.tldr: π₀-PSRL separates deciding when exploration is needed from choosing how to explore, yielding instance-dependent regret guarantees for episodic MDPs.

papers.abstract: Once historical clients become unavailable, a federation must serve newcomers through the artifact it leaves behind. How much of its knowledge remains useful in an architecture chosen afterward? We introduce FEDNBO, a seven-dataset benchmark that separates knowledge supply, policy identification, and private-model compilation under disjoint data roles. Controlled studies expose inflated oracle gains, architecture-dependent transfer reversals, and a gap between teacher accuracy and private-model utility. Ordinary public-response distillation provides a competitive reference without public task labels or newcomer samples: gains over strengthened local training are 23.52 and 16.62 percentage points on 300 CelebA identities and 300 FedEMNIST writers, respectively. In a complete-pipeline FedEMNIST comparison, this reference reaches 97.13% accuracy with 12.4 seconds of compilation per architecture, versus 97.03% and 67.5 seconds for a HeteroFedTTA reconstruction at the same epoch budget. Equal-count public-input interventions extend support sensitivity to trainable visual backbones. Together, these results establish an auditable benchmark and a strong reference for evaluating the utility, cost and reliability of post-federation knowledge transfer.
authors: Xinyuan Zhao
bullets: Separates knowledge supply, policy identification, and private-model compilation using disjoint data roles across seven datasets.
Finds inflated oracle gains, architecture-dependent transfer reversals, and a mismatch between teacher accuracy and private-model utility.

Ordinary public-response distillation is a competitive reference without public labels or newcomer samples, improving over strengthened local training by 23.52 and 16.62 percentage points on CelebA and FedEMNIST, respectively.
On FedEMNIST, it achieves 97.13% accuracy with 12.4 seconds of compilation per architecture, compared with 97.03% and 67.5 seconds for HeteroFedTTA at the same epoch budget.
Equal-count public-input interventions assess support sensitivity for trainable visual backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FEDNBO, a benchmark for knowledge portability to heterogeneous newcomers in federated learning. Relevant to continual and online learning.
papers.title: After the Federation: Benchmarking Knowledge Portability to Heterogeneous Newcomers
papers.tldr: FEDNBO benchmarks how effectively a federation’s remaining knowledge can be transferred to heterogeneous newcomer architectures after historical clients disappear.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has improved video reasoning in multimodal large language models. However, standard video GRPO varies only linguistic trajectories while conditioning every rollout in a group on the same sampled frames, which can produce homogeneous rewards and weaken group-relative learning when the shared visual evidence is insufficient or distracting. We propose \textbf{FrameGRPO}, a simple and effective reinforcement-learning framework that requires neither auxiliary networks nor changes to the model architecture. Specifically, FrameGRPO combines two lightweight components: (1) \textbf{Multi-Frame Rollouts}, which use only uniform temporal subsampling of a single maximal-frame decode to construct aligned views that diversify visual evidence and reasoning trajectories; and (2) \textbf{Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit}, which selectively reinforces a correct lower-ratio trajectory when all rollouts in a fixed full-ratio reference subset fail, without imposing an unconditional preference for fewer frames. Extensive experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate robust overall improvements over standard GRPO, highlighting temporal-view diversification as an effective mechanism for exploration and credit assignment in video MLLMs.
authors: Jiaxuan Sun, Biao Wang, Shuai Li
bullets: Standard video GRPO gives every rollout the same frames, which can cause homogeneous rewards and weak group-relative learning.
Multi-Frame Rollouts create aligned, temporally subsampled views from one maximal-frame decode to diversify visual evidence without architectural changes.
Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit rewards a correct lower-frame-ratio trajectory only when all full-ratio reference rollouts fail.
Experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks show robust improvements over standard GRPO.
The method uses no auxiliary networks or model-architecture modifications.
papers.selection_reason: RL framework for video reasoning in MLLMs with multi-frame rollouts; fits video understanding and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: FrameGRPO: Incentivizing Video Reasoning via Multi-Frame Rollouts and Temporal Credit
papers.tldr: FrameGRPO improves video reasoning by diversifying sampled temporal views during GRPO training and selectively rewarding efficient correct solutions.

papers.abstract: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. It is the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. Using our GPU-accelerated pipeline, we translate curated English documents, assess translation quality, and repair low-quality outputs while preserving technical content and document structure and maintaining source traceability. Through continued-pretraining experiments across twelve languages, we show that combining our synthetic corpus with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline. Additional experiments show how data volume, script coverage, and Indic training share affect English performance. We also introduce the Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, a multilingual benchmark suite for evaluating Indic language models across chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation. The suite combines existing Indic benchmarks with task-aware translations of English benchmarks, using automated quality assessment, targeted correction, and native-speaker review in a human-in-the-loop pipeline. We use the suite to comprehensively benchmark contemporary open-weight Indic and multilingual models across capabilities and languages, revealing substantial variation across tasks and languages. Together, these resources provide a scalable foundation for developing and evaluating more capable Indic language models.
authors: Abhinav Khattar (NVIDIA), Aishwarya Chhabra (NVIDIA), Ameya Velingker (NVIDIA), Anusha Kamath (NVIDIA), Brandon Norick (NVIDIA), Kanishk Singla (NVIDIA), Kiran Praveen (NVIDIA), Markus Kliegl (NVIDIA), Mohammad Qazim Bhat (NVIDIA), Mostofa Patwary (NVIDIA), Niket Agarwal (NVIDIA), Rajpreet Thethy (NVIDIA), Ramani Akkati (NVIDIA), Raviraj Joshi (NVIDIA), Sai Nishanth Padala (NVIDIA), Shuoyang Ding (NVIDIA), Sriharsha Niverty (NVIDIA), Utkarsh Vaidya (NVIDIA), Vitaly Lavrukhin (NVIDIA), Yev Meyer (NVIDIA), Anoop Kunchukuttan (AI4Bharat), Mitesh Khapra (AI4Bharat), Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan (AI4Bharat), Rudra Murthy (AI4Bharat), Sumanth Doddapaneni (AI4Bharat), Thanmay Jayakumar (AI4Bharat), Ujjwal Sharma (AI4Bharat)
bullets: The corpus contains approximately 2.83 trillion tokens across all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native scripts and 12 in romanized form.
A GPU-accelerated pipeline translates curated English data, evaluates and repairs low-quality outputs, preserves structure and technical content, and maintains source traceability.
Continued-pretraining experiments across 12 languages find that combining synthetic data with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline.
The Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite covers chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation using translated benchmarks plus native-speaker review.
Benchmarking open-weight models reveals substantial variation across tasks and languages; experiments also examine data volume, script coverage, and Indic-data share effects on English performance.
papers.selection_reason: Large-scale synthetic pretraining corpus and evaluation suite for Indic LLMs, relevant to LLM pretraining and evaluation.
papers.title: Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs
papers.tldr: The work releases a large synthetic Indic pretraining corpus and multilingual evaluation suite to support scalable development and assessment of Indic LLMs.

papers.abstract: Thin cylindrical objects offer little space for planar markers. We propose a dual-colour-stripe marker that uses the known curvature of an object to improve pose measurement with a single camera. The boundary between two colours provides a long centre line, while dots and printed edges supply features at different depths. We analyse how this depth separation improves the estimation of rotation about the cylinder axis, or roll. For a camera-facing marker at 15 cm, the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound on roll standard deviation is 2.00{\deg}for a flat marker, 0.38{\deg}for a single curved marker and 0.21{\deg}for a wrap-around marker. Monte Carlo roll RMS errors are within about 10% of the corresponding standard-deviation bounds. A first-order relation connects the sagitta of the curved marker to the roll sensitivity provided by a stereo baseline. The analytical and simulation results explain how curvature improves monocular measurement and provide a basis for designing marker geometry.
authors: Jaesung Hong, Dong Won Lee
bullets: The marker addresses the limited space available for planar markers on thin cylinders.
Its colour boundary provides a long centre line, while dots and printed edges offer features at different depths.
Analysis relates curvature-induced depth separation to improved rotation-about-axis (roll) sensitivity.
At 15 cm, the roll standard-deviation bound is 2.00° for a flat marker, 0.38° for a curved marker, and 0.21° for a wrap-around marker.
Monte Carlo errors closely match the analytical bounds, supporting marker-geometry design based on curvature.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a dual-colour-stripe marker for monocular pose estimation of cylinders using curvature. Relevant to 3D perception and geometry.
papers.title: Curvature as a Baseline: Monocular Pose Measurement of Cylindrical Objects with Dual Colour Stripe Markers
papers.tldr: A dual-colour stripe marker exploits cylindrical curvature and depth separation to substantially improve monocular roll estimation on thin cylindrical objects.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential for time series reasoning, while models that reason over time series are usually with long chains of thought. However, this process often consumes thousands of tokens, directly leading to substantial latency during inference. In contrast, System 1 models such as Jev make decisions instantly and can naturally be an alternative, but raw time series are not compatible with the embedding space of these models, thus hindering the reasoning performance, especially when input series contain thousands of numeric points. In this paper, we make a very early attempt to propose a time series System 1 model, namely TimesJev. Specifically, we first formalize System 1 sufficiency in time series reasoning, which motivates a compressed representation for time series with key frequency patterns preserved. To construct this representation, we derive a dimension reduction objective that combines (i) a sufficiency divergence that measures the core information lost during compression, and (ii) a realizability divergence that quantifies the incompatibility of the System 1 model to the optimal prediction given this representation. We optimize this objective by learning time series compression with a gating mechanism for sufficiency, and then aligning the selected representation with the embedding space for realizability. Finally, experiments on 13 datasets demonstrate that TimesJev outperforms reasoning models by over 62% with 62.9% less inference time than their fine-tuned versions on average.
authors: Chenghao Liu, Wei Fan, Jindong Han, Dongjie Wang, Aniket Mahanti, Pengyang Wang, Hao Liu
bullets: Targets the high latency of long chain-of-thought reasoning over lengthy time series.
Defines System 1 sufficiency and compresses series while retaining important frequency patterns.
Combines sufficiency and realizability divergences to guide compression and embedding alignment.
Uses a gating mechanism to select sufficient information and align it with the System 1 model’s embedding space.
Across 13 datasets, it reportedly outperforms reasoning models by over 62% while reducing inference time by 62.9% versus fine-tuned versions.
papers.selection_reason: System 1 time-series reasoning model reduces inference latency versus long chain-of-thought.
papers.title: TimesJev: Thinking Fast on Time Series with System 1 Sufficiency
papers.tldr: TimesJev enables fast time-series reasoning by compressing signals into System 1-compatible representations while preserving key information.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) for complex tasks, yet often overthink easy inputs, increasing token cost and latency, and sometimes degrading accuracy. Existing methods optimize reasoning length during training or impose external control at inference, but leave the underlying reasoning mechanism a black box. We find that fast and slow thinking exhibit distinct expert-routing patterns: holding the input fixed and varying only the prompted reasoning tempo produces stable routing shifts. Suppressing slow-thinking experts shortens the reasoning chain, whereas suppressing fast-thinking experts lengthens it, providing causal evidence that these experts influence reasoning depth. Based on this finding, we propose TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework. It identifies fast- and slow-thinking experts via tempo-contrastive routing analysis and redistributes routing weights within the original top-k set according to sample difficulty. It amplifies fast-thinking experts and suppresses slow-thinking experts on easy inputs and reverses this adjustment on hard ones, enabling difficulty-adaptive control over reasoning depth. We evaluate TempoMoE on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE consistently improves accuracy while reducing output tokens, with accuracy gains of up to 2.6 points and token reductions of up to 35.4%.
authors: Xiyue Zhang, Keru Zhou, Ziyi Wang, Bing Hu, Li Wang
bullets: Identifies distinct expert-routing patterns associated with fast versus slow reasoning and shows they causally affect chain-of-thought depth.
Uses a training-free, two-stage tempo-contrastive analysis to identify these experts.
Redistributes routing weights within the original top-k experts based on input difficulty: favoring fast experts for easy inputs and slow experts for hard ones.
Evaluated on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks, improving accuracy by up to 2.6 points and reducing output tokens by up to 35.4%.
Scope: controls reasoning depth through expert routing without changing model training.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free expert routing steering for efficient multimodal reasoning; reduces token cost and latency in MLLMs.
papers.title: TempoMoE: Identifying and Steering Fast-Slow Thinking Experts for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: TempoMoE adaptively steers fast- and slow-thinking experts to reduce unnecessary multimodal reasoning while improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought. For a prescribed loop count $L=L(n)$ and a fixed integer $k\ge1$ satisfying $s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L)$, our transformer simulates a time-$t(n)$, space-$s(n)$ Turing machine using a context window of $O(s(n)/L)$ and $O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L)$ generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of $L$ relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.
authors: Kehang Zhou, Pinyan Lu
bullets: Bridges explicit CoT, which uses generated tokens, and latent thought, which uses recurrence in hidden states.
For loop count L=L(n) and fixed k≥1 with s(n)^(1/k)=Ω(L), the model simulates a time-t(n), space-s(n) Turing machine.
Uses context window O(s(n)/L) and O(t(n)s(n)^(1/k)/L) generated tokens.
These resources are each reduced by a factor of L relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation.
The construction also works with constant-bit-size softmax attention under the paper’s finite-precision kernel.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical construction of looped transformers that internalize chain-of-thought, reducing context and generated tokens; relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: A constant-bit-size looped transformer can internalize chain-of-thought into recurrent hidden-state computation while reducing context and generated-token requirements by a factor of the loop count.

papers.abstract: Large language models remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks requiring procedural reasoning. We argue that a key cause is the absence of explicit procedural memory: accessible, modifiable knowledge of how tasks are accomplished, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. Goal-Oriented Graphs offer such a representation, encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable symbolic structure. We examine their construction, the challenges they pose, and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning.
authors: Jonathan Leung, Zhiqi Shen, Deheng Ye
bullets: Long-horizon procedural reasoning remains unreliable in large language models.
Procedural memory is proposed as distinct from semantic and episodic memory.
Goal-Oriented Graphs encode goals and prerequisite dependencies in inspectable symbolic structures.
The paper examines graph construction challenges and principles for integrating symbolic structure with neural reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Explicit procedural memory for language agents via goal-oriented graphs; relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Procedural Memory for Language Agents: A Neurosymbolic Perspective on Explicit Goal Structure
papers.tldr: The paper argues that explicit, modifiable procedural memory represented as Goal-Oriented Graphs could improve language agents’ reliability on long-horizon procedural tasks.

papers.abstract: Designing capable neural policies for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF), which map local observations to action distributions, represents an important challenge in multi-agent learning, with practical relevance to scalable collective automation problems such as warehouse logistics. In contrast to prior studies focusing primarily on individual policy design, this study explores a meta-level Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approach to learning-based MAPF. Specifically, given a collection of compact yet high-performing experts specialised for different map distributions, our architecture learns a router that selectively fuses their outputs according to each agent's local situation. We instantiate and validate this MoE approach with a commonly used graph neural network-based policy as well as a newly developed recursive action-token refinement model. Combined with supervised and reinforcement learning fine-tuning of the experts, our experiments show that MoE generally improves upon the pretrained policy and outperforms existing leading methods. At the same time, our findings reveal that appropriately trained, parameter-matched monolithic models still outperform MoE, highlighting a nuanced role for map-distribution MoE for MAPF.
authors: Fumimaro Suzuki, Keisuke Okumura
bullets: Targets scalable multi-agent pathfinding for settings such as warehouse logistics.
Learns a router to selectively fuse compact experts specialized for different map distributions.
Evaluates the approach with a graph neural network policy and a recursive action-token refinement model.
Uses supervised learning and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning for the experts.
MoE generally improves pretrained policies and surpasses existing leading methods, but parameter-matched monolithic models perform better.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based multi-agent pathfinding with mixture-of-experts; relevant to robot navigation policies.
papers.title: Map-Distribution Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
papers.tldr: A map-distribution Mixture-of-Experts router combines specialized MAPF policies by local situation, improving pretrained policies while remaining behind well-trained monolithic models.

papers.abstract: Tool-use agents pay per decision: at each hop a language model re-reads the state and thinks for seconds, though its actions are finite and decisions recur. We present NIOCIS, a routing layer that folds execution logs into a loop-collapsed action graph (forward transitions plus recovery back-edges) answering one typed question: which declared option at a state, plus stop, does the fleet take next? A small model reads a calibrated distribution over them in one pass, emitting no text. On 1,615 production security-operations episodes we measure what the layer replaces, returns and is bounded by. Replaces: the typed encoder matches the logged next hop on 32.2% of the 3,875 held-out decisions (34.9% within the declared options) in 10 ms of encoder time (19.5 ms for the typed-choice form), against 2.2 s per LLM hop; two feature readouts reach 32.8% and 32.3%, an ordering the paired test does not resolve, so the typed layer is chosen for cost, not a separated lead. Tuning: jpt-4b reaches 9.9% zero-shot and 31.9% fine-tuned, a gap an exact paired test does not resolve (p=0.68), at 244 ms. Returns little: the realised hop falls outside the declared options for 7.9% of decisions and outside the model's top twenty for 9.3%; the most confident 15% holds 91.9% accuracy. Bounded: a cross-trace leave-one-out test puts the released state's ceiling at 25.6--44.9% as the state key grows more specific, i.e. repeated states disagree more often than they agree; the option-space ablation attributes the gain to per-node candidate restriction (+3.5 points over a flat catalog) rather than graph traversal (zero within its interval); a gated self-evolution loop lifts every arm above its anchor yet ends below full supervision; a confidence-gated cascade loses agreement when the escalation arm is the zero-shot stand-in; and agreement past a third of the fleet needs a state carrying the plan and the observation.
authors: Jin Han, Mingfeng Xin, Feng Liang, Jingtao Yu
bullets: Builds a loop-collapsed action graph with forward transitions and recovery back-edges, then predicts the next declared option or stop in one pass without generating text.
On 3,875 held-out decisions, the typed encoder matched logged next hops on 32.2% overall and 34.9% within declared options, versus roughly 2.2 seconds per LLM hop.
Node-conditioned candidate restriction contributed a +3.5-point gain over a flat catalog; graph traversal showed no measurable additional gain within the reported interval.
Behavior is difficult to reproduce: 7.9% of realized hops were outside declared options, and repeated states often disagreed, limiting the state-conditioned ceiling to 25.6–44.9%.
The most confident 15% of predictions reached 91.9% accuracy, while broader agreement above one-third of the fleet required state information containing both the plan and observation.
papers.selection_reason: Routing layer replacing expensive LLM hops with small-model decisions; reduces latency and token cost, fits efficient AI.
papers.title: NIOCIS: Typed-Decision Next-Hop Routing with Node-Conditioned Option Spaces for Tool-Use Agents
papers.tldr: NIOCIS accelerates tool-use routing by predicting a typed next action from a node-specific option set, replacing costly LLM decisions with millisecond-scale inference but achieving only partial agreement with logged behavior.

papers.abstract: Multi-hop question answering (QA) requires models to chain intermediate conclusions while remaining cost-aware. Existing training-free self-reflective protocols (generate -> critique -> revise) improve accuracy but operate on a flat token stream: revisions cannot identify which prior step is unreliable, and early stopping cannot exploit structural convergence. We introduce GraphEvoResearcher, a training-free protocol that lifts EvoResearcher's self-reflective meta-reward onto an explicit reasoning graph - nodes are intermediate conclusions/evidence and edges encode support, contradict, and depends_on. A graph-aware meta-reward combines correctness, efficiency, reflection, diversity, and four structural signals (connectivity, acyclicity, branch coverage, path convergence) to decide whether to revise, backtrack, or stop. A graph-convergence early-stop terminates when evidence branches converge on a single conclusion. On a real LLM (DeepSeek), over GSM8K, MATH, and BBH (n=50 each), GraphEvoResearcher reaches 98%, 92%, and 82% respectively, the highest of all baselines, with the largest gains on the hardest set (MATH: +24 pp over single-shot, +12 pp over flat reflection), while keeping construction cost bounded at ~2 steps / 4.5-5 nodes. Our results indicate the structural signal of a reasoning graph is most valuable exactly where single-step reasoning is unreliable.
authors: Suxing Liu
bullets: Addresses flat generate–critique–revise protocols, which cannot localize unreliable reasoning steps or exploit structural convergence.
Represents intermediate conclusions and evidence as graph nodes with support, contradiction, and dependency edges.
Uses graph-aware rewards covering correctness, efficiency, reflection, diversity, connectivity, acyclicity, branch coverage, and path convergence.
On DeepSeek across GSM8K, MATH, and BBH (50 examples each), achieves 98%, 92%, and 82%, respectively; MATH gains are +24 percentage points over single-shot and +12 over flat reflection.
Keeps construction cost bounded at approximately 2 steps and 4.5–5 nodes; evaluation is limited to the reported model and benchmark samples.
papers.selection_reason: Graph-aware self-reflective reasoning with structural early stopping reduces reasoning cost.
papers.title: GraphEvoResearcher: Graph-Aware Training-Free Self-Reflective Reasoning for Cost-Bounded Multi-Hop Question Answering
papers.tldr: GraphEvoResearcher improves cost-bounded multi-hop QA by using a self-reflective reasoning graph to target revisions and stop when evidence converges.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve problem solving, but models often keep generating after the correct answer is already reachable; the extra steps raise serving costs and may replace a correct intermediate result with an incorrect one. We propose GLOBE (Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit), an online, training-free algorithm that terminates the model's CoT process early. GLOBE embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and reads the shape of the resulting semantic trajectory. GLOBE first applies a trial phase that generates short trial answers in a separate branch, stopping the main stream on an accepted trial after checking confidence against a threshold. If generation continues, a trajectory phase stops the stream once this path repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. On five benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, tool calling, and agent memory, GLOBE cuts output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time (E2E) by 51.0% across two models, and achieves a five-task average of 80.58%, comparable to Full CoT.
authors: Xinyue Peng, Zhenlin Liang, Meng Cai, Hua Wang
bullets: Addresses unnecessary CoT generation, which increases serving cost and can turn correct intermediate reasoning into incorrect final answers.
Embeds completed reasoning segments on a unit sphere and analyzes their semantic trajectory online.
Uses a trial phase with short branch answers and confidence thresholds, followed by a trajectory phase that detects repeated reversals with little progress.
Across five tasks and two models, reduces output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time by 51.0%.
Achieves an 80.58% five-task average, comparable to Full CoT.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free early exit for chain-of-thought reduces output tokens and latency, fitting efficient inference.
papers.title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories
papers.tldr: GLOBE is a training-free early-exit method that uses confidence checks and geometric trajectory patterns to stop chain-of-thought reasoning earlier, reducing computation while preserving Full-CoT-level performance.

papers.abstract: Most existing approaches to LLM swarm optimization are utility-driven, focusing on final task utility while leaving the processing, integration, and reliance of information within individual interactions largely implicit. To address this, we study LLM swarm interactions from an information-flow-based view and introduce behavioral probes to quantify information flow patterns. Specifically, we repurpose External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS)---originally designed for hallucination analysis---to measure a node's external-context dependence and parametric-knowledge dependence, respectively. Across controlled and realistic swarm settings, we observe consistent patterns: ECS increases with input relevance and distinguishes useful multi-source contributions, while PKS decreases as informative context accumulates. Building on this heuristic interpretation, we demonstrate how these probes can complement utility-driven structure optimization in two controlled applications. Probe-guided node pruning reduces redundant communication and token consumption, and probe-guided reasoning-path search accelerates convergence compared to utility-only baselines. Our empirical results suggest that behavioral probes can make the internal information flow of LLM swarms observable and serve as effective auxiliary signals for structure optimization.
authors: Junhui Chen, Yu Zhang, Lantian Li, Dong Wang
bullets: Reframes swarm analysis from final utility to how agents process, integrate, and rely on information.
Uses ECS to measure external-context dependence and PKS to measure parametric-knowledge dependence.
ECS rises with input relevance and captures useful multi-source contributions, while PKS falls as informative context accumulates.
Probe-guided pruning reduces redundant communication and token use; probe-guided path search accelerates convergence versus utility-only baselines.
Demonstrates probes as auxiliary signals for swarm structure optimization across controlled and realistic settings.
papers.selection_reason: Probe-guided pruning reduces token consumption and communication in LLM swarms; transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: Behavioral Probes for Information Flow in LLM Swarms
papers.tldr: Behavioral probes based on ECS and PKS make information flow in LLM swarms measurable and support more efficient communication and reasoning-path optimization.

papers.abstract: We set out to reproduce a recent hallucination-mitigation result on the POPE benchmark. The LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline we measured, 82.21 F1 on the adversarial split, sat 1.21 to 8.67 points above the adversarial baselines we planned to compare against (81.00, 79.30, and 73.54).
