We looked at the evaluation code and found a readout choice that moves F1 on its own. A two-token logit readout decides yes versus no by comparing two vocabulary IDs, 3582 ("yes") and 1217 ("no"). Across 9,000 greedy-decode questions spanning all three splits, neither ID is generated even once. The model emits " Yes" (token 3869) and " No" (token 1939), because SentencePiece prepends a space byte after the prompt suffix "ASSISTANT:". Read with an eight-token lookup that covers the space-prefixed surface forms, LLaVA-1.5-7B scores F1 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on the adversarial, popular, and random splits. That 6.13-point adversarial shift exceeds the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed. None of them states its readout, and our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, so we cannot say how much of any reported gain a matched evaluation would keep. That comparison stays unresolved until readout and precision are matched. On the fixed baseline we run nine inference-time corrections of our own (none beat it) and dissect why the adversarial split resists logit-level intervention. In a 3,000-question probe, wrong predictions draw more image attention than correct ones (Cohen's $d=-0.46$, $p=1.4\times10^{-24}$), the opposite of what grounding-based corrections assume. A four-readout audit across four further VLMs from three tokenizer families confirms the confound is protocol-level, not model-specific: porting the LLaVA-1.5 IDs verbatim drops F1 to 0.00 on the two disjoint-vocabulary models, whereas a tokenizer-derived readout holds between 0.80 and 0.92.
authors: Kesav Kumar Jayakumar, Karthigeyan Thilak
bullets: A two-token readout using unspaced “yes”/“no” IDs never matches LLaVA-1.5-7B’s generated space-prefixed tokens, distorting evaluation.
A tokenizer-derived eight-token readout yields LLaVA-1.5-7B F1 scores of 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on adversarial, popular, and random splits.
The adversarial readout shift is larger than gains reported by five of six surveyed papers, but comparisons remain unresolved because precision and readout settings differ.
Across four additional VLMs, copying LLaVA’s IDs causes F1 to fall to 0.00 for two models, while tokenizer-specific readouts produce 0.80–0.92.
Nine tested inference-time corrections did not improve the fixed baseline; attention analysis also challenges assumptions behind grounding-based interventions.
papers.selection_reason: Systematic audit of VLM hallucination evaluation (POPE) revealing tokenization confounds. Directly relevant to Multimodal Large Language Models.
papers.title: Token-Set Choice Confounds POPE: A Systematic Audit of Yes/No Extraction in VLM Hallucination Evaluation
papers.tldr: POPE hallucination scores can be substantially confounded by using the wrong tokenizer-specific yes/no token IDs, making readout protocol matching essential.

papers.abstract: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions. To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
authors: Hojin Jeon, Jimin Lee, Taekwan Kim, Nayoung Oh, Taeyoung Kim, Myungkyu Koo, Jinmo Koo, Joonwoo Ahn, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses temporal inefficiency caused by fine-grained actions learned from teleoperation data.
Uses shared-expert action decoders supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons.
Selects execution modes through quantizability guidance and a context-conditioned router.
Improves execution efficiency while maintaining success across three simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks.
Evaluated on multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive temporal action quantization for VLA robot policies; directly fits vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: PaceVLA adaptively varies action granularity in VLA policies to speed up robot manipulation without sacrificing task success.

papers.abstract: Joint 4D reconstruction of a human and object from a monocular video is essential for understanding how people interact with their environment. While recent methods have made noticeable progress, capturing such human-object interactions remains difficult due to two main challenges. First, a video typically contains composite semantic context spanning multiple interaction phases, making it difficult to track the temporal changes of the interaction in the reconstruction. Second, under human-object occlusion, a single-view observation contains incomplete visual information about the interaction, resulting in geometrically inconsistent reconstructions. To address these challenges, we introduce HORIA, built upon two core designs. First, we decompose the entire input video into temporally grounded and semantically distinct interaction phases with motion-aware captioning, obtaining a specific text description for each phase. Second, conditioned on these text descriptions of the interaction, we propose an interaction-aware re-rendering that compensates for the limited single-view observation. Specifically, we render the initially reconstructed 4D human and object from novel viewpoints and refine the renderings with a text-to-video diffusion prior, which provides auxiliary novel-view supervision beyond single-view cues. As a result, our framework produces temporally coherent and accurate 4D reconstructions under diverse interaction scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Hyeongjin Nam, Taeryung Lee, Daniel Sungho Jung, Kyoung Mu Lee
bullets: Addresses interaction-phase changes and incomplete geometry caused by human-object occlusion in single-view video.
Decomposes videos into semantically distinct, temporally grounded phases using motion-aware captioning.
Uses phase descriptions to guide text-to-video diffusion refinement of novel-view renderings.
Provides auxiliary supervision beyond the original monocular observations.
Reports accurate, temporally coherent reconstructions across diverse interactions with state-of-the-art performance.
papers.selection_reason: Reconstructs 4D human and object scenes from monocular video using interaction-aware re-rendering. This advances 3D reconstruction and world modeling for embodied interactions.
papers.title: HORIA: 4D Human and Object Reconstruction from a Monocular Video with Interaction-Aware Re-Rendering
papers.tldr: HORIA reconstructs temporally coherent 4D humans and objects from monocular interaction videos by combining phase-aware text descriptions with diffusion-guided novel-view re-rendering.

papers.abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.
authors: X. Feng, J. Tang, Z. Lin, L. Chen, S. Shao, Q. Lu, K. Huang
bullets: Targets embodied agents that can understand diverse 3D environments and perform general actions beyond single-scene tasks.
Provides over 200K navigation-planning samples across diverse scenes with low-level motion and high-level semantic annotations.
Introduces unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics for offline pretraining and fair assessment.
Uses a video world model as a low-cost proxy environment for interactive RL post-training.
Pretraining improves open-world planning, while world-model RL further improves performance on out-of-distribution scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied navigation-planning dataset with interactive video world models for RL post-training directly fits embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: EmbodiedWorld-200K advances open-world embodied agents with a 200K-sample planning dataset and video-world-model-based interactive RL.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.
authors: Rui Wang, Zishen Lai, Jiayu Liu, Cheng Qian, Jeonghwan Kim, Heng Wang, Xuejun Zhang, Jiateng Liu, Bingxuan Li, Shujin Wu, Qing Zong, Tianshi Zheng, Chunyang Li, Qihan Lin, Chen Li, Dadi Guo, Xiusi Chen, Yangqiu Song
bullets: Benchmarks proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments.
Agents must infer hidden rules from evidence and detect implicit rule drift through degraded performance.
Experiments across eight leading LLMs show the task remains challenging; GPT-6 Sol reaches 61.9% calibrated accuracy.
Providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance by nearly 10%.
Agents often reason well with informative evidence but struggle to obtain the right evidence and recognize when prior evidence is outdated.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for LLM agents' proactive exploration and test-time adaptation under rule drift; fits test-time learning.
papers.title: AdaExploreBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Proactive Exploration and Test-time Adaptation in Evolving Environments
papers.tldr: AdaExploreBench tests whether LLM agents can proactively discover hidden environmental rules and adapt when those rules silently change, revealing major weaknesses in evidence acquisition and stale-knowledge detection.

papers.abstract: Generative modeling of discrete data has two popular paradigms: autoregressive models such as GPT, which factorize a sequence in a left-to-right (L2R) order, and masked diffusion models, which are essentially any-order autoregressive modeling. Rather than competing methods, these are the two extreme points of a single axis -- the generation order. For structured discrete domains without a natural traversal, both extremes may be suboptimal, yet the intermediate choice -- a single well-adapted order -- remains largely unexplored. We introduce OrderGPT, which builds on Any-Order GPT to learn a task-level generation order without canonical-order supervision. Our key observation is that predicting variables from randomly sampled reveal prefixes produces recurring attention patterns in the backbone that provide a model-dependent signal of predictive dependencies. We aggregate this signal into a reciprocal dependency graph and use a spectral teacher to derive continuous generation priorities. A lightweight OrderMLP integrated into the GPT backbone learns to predict these priorities from attention, incorporating order learning into the architecture within a single training run. Training gradually shifts toward the learned order, which is then frozen for subsequent autoregressive training and generation. The same mechanism adapts across modalities: adaptively it recovers near-L2R dependency structure in language, learns anatomically organized factorizations on human pose, and discovers a factorization on tabular data that places statistically and semantically related fields nearby, while improving downstream modeling metrics across all domains. The code is available at https://github.com/Chenhe-yang/OrderGPT/.
authors: Chenhe Yang, Yuhuan Lyu, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Targets structured domains where neither left-to-right nor fully arbitrary generation order is ideal.
Extracts predictive dependencies from attention patterns under randomly sampled reveal prefixes.
Builds a reciprocal dependency graph and uses a spectral teacher to produce continuous generation priorities.
An OrderMLP learns these priorities within the GPT backbone during a single training run, after which the order is frozen.
Adapts across language, human pose, and tabular data, improving downstream modeling metrics across these domains.
papers.selection_reason: Learnable generation order for GPT-style models is a meaningful architectural contribution relevant to LLM foundation models.
papers.title: OrderGPT: Generation Order as a Learnable Modeling Choice
papers.tldr: OrderGPT learns a task-specific generation order for discrete data, bridging fixed-order autoregressive and any-order masked diffusion models.

papers.abstract: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.
authors: Matthias Eder, Pantelis Emmanouil, Vivek Farias, Fabian Fischer, Adam Jozefiak, Tianyi Peng, Thomas Ulz, Raphael Watschinger, Fangyu Wu, Andrew Zheng
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between labor-intensive algorithm design and opaque task-specific reinforcement learning.
Coding agents iteratively propose, implement, simulate, diagnose, verify, and refine policies in code space.
Two case studies found policies outperforming manually engineered or proprietary baselines, including reported gains of 35.0% and 58.9%.
The warehouse algorithm forms a new class of method and is proven collision-free and finite-completion under stated assumptions.
Results are demonstrated on competition maps and simulated irregular-lane warehouses; guarantees depend on the stated assumptions.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-agent pathfinding policy search with coding agents; directly relevant to embodied robot navigation and planning.
papers.title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
papers.tldr: Human-directed coding-agent search can discover interpretable, high-performing multi-agent pathfinding policies with formal correctness guarantees.

papers.abstract: Offline compaction of the key--value cache (KV-cache) reduces the cost of repeatedly querying a fixed context by constructing a smaller cache once and reusing it subsequently. The central challenge of compaction is deciding which cache entries to delete and which to retain. Existing methods score each candidate for deletion on its own, with the rest of the cache being held fixed. However, softmax renormalization of the attention operation couples these decisions in a nonlinear manner: removing one entry changes the attention weights of every remaining one. In this work, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses calibration data to take interactions into account in a tractable way. We derive a quadratic surrogate that admits closed-form expressions for jointly making the optimal greedy removal decision as well as compensation within the remaining entries. On QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, and at every evaluated compaction ratio, KV-Surgeon substantially advances the cost--accuracy Pareto frontier of dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters. At $50\times$ compaction, KV-Surgeon improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), the state of the art, at comparable cost. Lastly, we introduce an even faster variant, which also exceeds the state of the art while requiring only two fifths of its cost.
authors: Moritz Wagner, Christophe Roux, Max Zimmer, Sebastian Pokutta
bullets: Existing methods evaluate cache entries independently, overlooking how deleting one entry changes attention over all others.
KV-Surgeon uses calibration data and a quadratic surrogate to jointly choose greedy deletions and compensate remaining entries.
It improves the cost–accuracy Pareto frontier across QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena for dense and mixture-of-experts models.
At 50× compaction, it improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching at comparable cost.
A faster variant also surpasses the prior state of the art at two-fifths of its cost.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets KV-cache compaction and memory-efficient LLM inference with compensation-aware offline pruning.
papers.title: The KV-Surgeon: Compensation-Aware Offline KV-Cache Compaction
papers.tldr: KV-Surgeon improves offline KV-cache compaction by modeling interactions caused by softmax renormalization, achieving better accuracy–cost tradeoffs than prior methods.

papers.abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.
authors: Minoo Ahmadi, Seyedarmin Azizi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: SMC enhances inference-time search by resampling partial generations according to internal confidence or external process rewards.
Multinomial resampling can duplicate high-weight candidates and eliminate alternative lineages, while ESS may miss this diversity loss.
LP-SMC combines Chopthin resampling with a weight floor to preserve unequal weights and give low-scoring lineages opportunities to recover.
Across two base models and multiple reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, LP-SMC improved oracle coverage in every setting and end-to-end accuracy in 11 of 12 settings.
Coverage gains also persisted with an external reward model, indicating separate benefits from diversity preservation and reward guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces diversity-preserving inference-time SMC decoding for diffusion LLMs, directly relevant to LLM decoding and reasoning.
papers.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Lineage-preserving SMC improves diffusion-LLM reasoning and code-generation decoding by maintaining diverse candidate trajectories during reward-guided resampling.

papers.abstract: In this work we focus on the problem of embodied task planning, which requires an agent to accomplish a complex task by separating it into atomic actions. Recent studies have developed LLM-based methods to address this problem. However, the executability and correctness of the generated plans remain suboptimal in complex environments and tasks. On the other hand, classical search algorithms have the potential to solve the planning problems perfectly, yet they require fully observable environments, known state transitions and goal state, which are often unattainable in general task domains. Therefore, we propose to implement an LLM-guided search algorithm that makes the search process possible and efficient by incorporating LLMs' commonsense knowledge. Our method leverages LLMs to (1) translate natural language instructions into formatted goal conditions, (2) facilitate efficient exploration in partially observable environments, (3) implement a rule-based world simulator, and (4) prune the space of candidate actions to improve search efficiency. Experimental results on VirtualHome and ALFWorld demonstrate its superior performance.
authors: Peiran Xu, Yixiang Yang, Jinghan Li, Fei Li, Cao Sheng, JiaZhong Yu, Yadong Mu
bullets: Addresses the limitations of LLM-generated plans and classical search when environments are complex, partially observable, or lack known transitions and goals.
Translates natural-language instructions into structured goal conditions and uses an LLM to guide exploration.
Employs a rule-based world simulator and prunes candidate actions to make search more efficient.
Demonstrates superior performance on the VirtualHome and ALFWorld benchmarks.
Scope: effectiveness is reported for these embodied task-planning environments; the abstract gives no further limitations.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-guided embodied task planning with search and simulation directly fits embodied AI.
papers.title: TESS: LLM-guided Translation, Exploration, Simulation, and Search for Embodied Task Planning
papers.tldr: TESS combines LLM commonsense reasoning with classical search to generate more executable and correct plans for embodied tasks in partially observable environments.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models can jointly understand video, audio, and text, yet they remain weak at temporal grounding, a capability essential for real-world audio-visual applications. To understand this limitation, we look beyond final predictions and examine the model's internal temporal evidence. We identify a temporal generation gap: the internal attention of the model localizes the target moment more accurately than the timestamps it generates. To close this gap, we propose TACG (Temporal Attention-Consistency Grounding), a post-training method that treats internal attention as a reliable temporal pivot and aligns it with both the model prediction and the ground-truth annotation through attention-consistency training. We further build a 580K-sample training dataset by reconstructing temporal QA from dense audio-visual annotations and organizing general omni-modal instruction data. Using TACG and this training dataset, we train OmniGround, a general-purpose omni-modal model with stronger temporal grounding capability, without injecting any additional temporal cues. OmniGround reaches state-of-the-art omni-modal temporal grounding, including 37.5 mIoU on LongVALE and 35.7 mIoU on UnAV-100, while staying competitive on both general audio-visual understanding and vision-only grounding.
authors: Zixuan Chen, Depeng Wang, Hao Lin, Ke Xu, Ya Guo, Huijia Zhu, Tanfeng Sun, Xinghao Jiang
bullets: Identifies a temporal generation gap: internal attention localizes target moments more accurately than generated timestamps.
Introduces TACG, a post-training attention-consistency method using internal attention as a temporal pivot.
Builds a 580K-sample dataset from dense audio-visual annotations and general omni-modal instructions.
Achieves 37.5 mIoU on LongVALE and 35.7 mIoU on UnAV-100, while remaining competitive in broader audio-visual and vision-only tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves temporal grounding in omni-modal LLMs using attention-consistency training. This advances multimodal temporal reasoning and video understanding.
papers.title: OmniGround: Strengthening Omni-Modal Temporal Grounding via Attention-Consistency Training
papers.tldr: OmniGround improves omni-modal video-audio-text temporal grounding by aligning internal attention with predicted and ground-truth timestamps.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation often depends on short-term cues - such as brief contacts, temporary occlusions, and intermediate object states - that are ambiguous in a single frame and can only be resolved by integrating observations over time. However, injecting historical information solely by enlarging the history window is computationally costly and frequently yields limited gains due to substantial redundancy and task-agnostic, inflexible sampling of observations. We propose CondenseVLA, a multi-frame VLA policy with a learnable decoder-side history condensation module for using short-term visual context in action decoding. Given a sequence of cached per-frame features from the VLM backbone, CondenseVLA distills observation history into a fixed set of slot tokens using learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention. Simple auxiliary regularization penalizes overlap among slot attention maps and decorrelates slot embeddings, encouraging complementary attention and reducing slot redundancy. Across the evaluated tasks, CondenseVLA improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8% (+11.1 percentage points), achieves 97.2% on LIBERO, and reaches 52.8% on real-world tasks. It achieves 21.6% success on memory-dependent RMBench tasks. These results support selective condensation of bounded recent visual evidence for action decoding, while harder multi-observation tasks expose the limits of a finite history window. Project page: https://github.com/FeiyangHong/CondenseVLA
authors: Feiyang Hong, Yujie Wei, Bo Zhao, Xiu Su, Hongxun Yao, Shuo Yang
bullets: Targets short-term cues such as contacts, occlusions, and intermediate object states that single frames cannot resolve.
Uses decoder-side learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention to compress cached per-frame VLM features into a fixed set of history slots.
Regularizes slot attention and embeddings to encourage complementary, non-redundant representations.
Improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8%, reaches 97.2% on LIBERO and 52.8% on real-world tasks.
Achieves 21.6% on memory-dependent RMBench tasks, highlighting limits of a finite recent-history window.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CondenseVLA, a VLA policy that condenses visual history into slot tokens for efficient robot manipulation. This directly addresses robot manipulation and embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: CondenseVLA: Learnable History Condensation for Efficient Multi-Frame VLA
papers.tldr: CondenseVLA efficiently integrates recent visual history into robot actions by learning to condense redundant frame features into complementary slot tokens.

papers.abstract: Deep research agents are increasingly capable of searching the open web and synthesizing evidence, yet they remain poorly suited to controllable report generation in multimodal deep research. This task requires agents to handle interleaved textual and visual inputs, gather multimodal evidence through multi-step web search, and deliver comprehensive illustrated reports under user-specified requirements. Existing systems face two limitations. During reasoning, they often underuse images discovered along the search trajectory; during generation, they tend to produce fixed-form answers with limited control over report granularity, multimodal composition, and evidence grounding. We introduce MIRA, a Multimodal Illustrated Deep Research Agent for controllable reports. MIRA integrates textual and visual evidence throughout research and writing. At its core, MIRA-Harness translates user requirements into generation contracts and connects four stages: evidence collection, report submission, feedback-driven revision, and final delivery. Building on this harness, MIRA-Data constructs high-quality multi-hop multimodal research trajectories, and we post-train foundation models to operate within the workflow. Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MIRA achieves state-of-the-art performance among open agents on 7 representative, established multimodal-search and deep-research-agent benchmarks, while producing user-aligned illustrated reports with traceable textual and visual evidence.
authors: Hongrui Wu, Kaiwen Tuo, Congcong Wang, Gen Li, Shuai Dong, Xinlei Yu, Yuqi Xu, Haowen Hou, Zelin Peng, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: Addresses weak image use during web research and limited control over report structure, granularity, and evidence grounding.
MIRA-Harness converts user requirements into generation contracts across evidence collection, submission, revision, and delivery.
MIRA-Data provides multi-hop multimodal research trajectories for post-training foundation models within this workflow.
Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MIRA achieves state-of-the-art results among open agents on seven multimodal-search and deep-research benchmarks.
Produces user-aligned illustrated reports grounded in traceable textual and visual evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces MIRA, a multimodal deep research agent for controllable reports. This involves multimodal reasoning and instruction following, relevant to multimodal and large language foundation models.
papers.title: MIRA: A Multimodal Illustrated Deep Research Agent for Controllable Reports
papers.tldr: MIRA is a multimodal deep-research agent that uses textual and visual evidence to generate controllable, illustrated reports with traceable citations.

papers.abstract: Video vision-language models (VLMs) have strong semantic understanding, yet remain unreliable at precise temporal grounding. Existing gains from explicitly aligning video frames with absolute time suggest that VLMs may already encode accurate temporal locations internally but lose precision when expressing them as timestamps. Our analysis across four VLMs and two grounding datasets confirms this hypothesis: attention intervals outperform predicted intervals on approximately 66% of valid examples. We term this discrepancy the temporal generation gap. Because precise temporal annotations are expensive, this finding motivates closing the gap to improve temporal grounding using only unlabeled video-query pairs. We propose Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses internal temporal attention as self-supervision for Group Relative Policy Optimization and applies a ground-truth-free criterion to select high-value samples. SAPO consistently improves temporal grounding across multiple datasets and models spanning weak to strong initial grounding ability. Relative mIoU gains reach 33.7% on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 5.4% on the strong Time-R1-7B. The improvements transfer across datasets while preserving general video understanding.
authors: Zixuan Chen, Depeng Wang, Wei Chen, Ke Xu, Ya Guo, Huijia Zhu, Tanfeng Sun, Xinghao Jiang
bullets: Identifies a temporal generation gap: attention-based intervals outperform model-predicted timestamps on about 66% of valid examples.
Trains with Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization, combining attention-derived supervision with Group Relative Policy Optimization.
Uses a ground-truth-free criterion to select high-value unlabeled video-query pairs.
Improves temporal grounding across datasets and VLMs, with relative mIoU gains of up to 33.7%.
Improvements transfer across datasets while preserving general video understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Improves temporal grounding in VLMs using self-supervised attention policy optimization (SAPO). This addresses temporal reasoning and video-language understanding.
papers.title: SAPO: Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization for Improving Temporal Video Grounding in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: SAPO uses a VLM’s internal temporal attention as self-supervision to improve precise video moment localization without labeled temporal annotations.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. These applications draw on three distinct long-context capabilities: recall, where the answer is a fact present in the context; state tracking, where the outcome can be computed by performing a series of transformations to a specified state; and pattern learning, where the goal is to make a prediction by sampling from a distribution inferred from many observations. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on the first capability. In this work, we introduce LEAPS (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking), a collection of 12 novel datasets, spanning agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and forecasting of market and world events. By construction, LEAPS is resistant to data contamination, extends to millions of input tokens, and uses reliable metrics. We evaluate 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens. LEAPS distinguishes models that perform near perfectly on recall tasks, finding that such models' state tracking and pattern learning abilities can vary significantly and degrade much more dramatically with increasing input lengths--even for pattern learning, where more observations should make learning a theoretically easier task. Moreover, thinking models often underperform their base counterparts, exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task. We hope LEAPS can guide the development of the next generation of LCLMs.
authors: Howard Yen, Nitya Mani, Alex Renda, Christopher S. Hardin
bullets: Introduces 12 datasets covering agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and market/world-event forecasting.
Tests recall, state tracking, and pattern learning across inputs up to millions of tokens.
Evaluates 30 API and open models with context lengths from 8K to 512K tokens.
Finds that models strong at recall can degrade sharply on state tracking and pattern learning with longer contexts.
Reports that thinking models can underperform base models by exhausting generation budgets or oversimplifying tasks.
papers.selection_reason: New benchmark for long-context capabilities (recall, state tracking, pattern learning) in LCLMs, directly relevant to long-context model evaluation.
papers.title: LEAPS: Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern Learning and State Tracking
papers.tldr: LEAPS evaluates long-context models beyond recall, revealing substantial weaknesses in state tracking and pattern learning as contexts grow.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models primarily rely on general-purpose ODE-based numerical methods for training-free accelerated sampling, but performance degrades with coarse time discretization. In this paper, we propose optimal linear leaps (LEAP), a specialized method grounded in theoretical and empirical investigations of sampling trajectory geometry. Built upon low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory consistency, LEAP formulates a supervised least-squares optimization problem within the local trajectory subspace, achieving a precise approximation of future states without model evaluations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LEAP outperforms previous methods across diverse modalities, including text-to-image (Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX.1-dev) and image-to-3D (TRELLIS.2) generation. Furthermore, LEAP can be seamlessly integrated into existing solver-based methods, offering a plug-and-play enhancement for modern diffusion models. Code is available at https://github.com/zju-pi/LEAP.
authors: Haowei Zheng, Zhenyu Zhou, Jiawei Chen, Can Wang, Defang Chen
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by coarse time discretization in accelerated diffusion sampling.
Uses low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory consistency to formulate a supervised least-squares optimization problem.
Approximates future sampling states without additional model evaluations.
Works across text-to-image and image-to-3D generation, including Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX.1-dev, and TRELLIS.2.
Can be integrated as a plug-and-play enhancement with existing solver-based methods.
papers.selection_reason: Accelerates ODE-based diffusion sampling with optimal linear leaps (LEAP). This improves inference efficiency for diffusion models, relevant to efficient AI and video diffusion.
papers.title: LEAP: Accelerating ODE-based Diffusion Sampling with Optimal Linear Leaps
papers.tldr: LEAP accelerates ODE-based diffusion sampling by predicting future states through optimal linear extrapolation in a local trajectory subspace, reducing the need for model evaluations.

papers.abstract: Sequential knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) often leads to a degradation of general capabilities due to cumulative parameter interference. In this paper, we revisit prominent projection-based methods like AlphaEdit and reveal a surprising mismatch: their robustness is primarily driven by update regularization rather than the intended null-space projection. Based on this insight, we propose FisherEdit, a theoretically grounded method built on Fisher geometry, which replaces coarse activation-space projections with importance-aware regularization in parameter space. It penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while retaining flexibility for new facts, and admits an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FisherEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance while better preserving model stability and downstream task accuracy.
authors: Yizhou Yang, Jiahong Fu, Zhiwu Wang, Kailong Fan, Haokun Lin, Yichen Wu, Zhenan Sun, Renzhen Wang, Deyu Meng
bullets: Sequential editing can cause cumulative parameter interference and degrade general abilities.
The paper finds that projection-based methods’ robustness mainly comes from update regularization, not null-space projection.
FisherEdit penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while allowing flexibility for new facts.
Its Fisher-geometry formulation has an efficient row-wise closed-form solution.
Experiments across Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 show strong performance and improved preservation of downstream accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Fisher information-guided knowledge editing for LLMs, addressing sequential editing and stability, relevant to model adaptation and memory.
papers.title: FisherEdit: Fisher Information Guided Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FisherEdit uses Fisher-information-guided parameter regularization to add knowledge while better preserving LLM stability and general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on challenging mathematical and scientific tasks through long chain-of-thought reasoning, but they often suffer from overthinking with unnecessary reasoning steps. Existing truncation-based methods typically detect consecutive trial-answer agreement and force early exit, yet such local stopping signals do not necessarily indicate final-answer stability and can disrupt useful subsequent reflection or verification, potentially leading to performance degradation. We propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding intervention for mitigating overthinking in LRMs. CALM first monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then applies logit masking to action transition point (ATP) tokens such as "Wait", "Alternatively", and "Hmm", suppressing redundant transitional reasoning while allowing the model to continue its thought process more naturally. Experiments across four advanced LRMs and five benchmarks show that CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%-25.0% compared with full CoT reasoning while maintaining performance, and can even improve accuracy by 0.07%-1.48% by reducing redundant reasoning. LLM-as-a-Judge results also demonstrate that CALM provides more coherent and concise results.
authors: Shengjing Liu, Feiyang Li, Yuxuan Yang, Yile Wang, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets overthinking caused by lengthy, redundant reasoning in large reasoning models.
Monitors trial-answer consistency at reasoning-step boundaries rather than forcing early termination.
Suppresses action transition point tokens such as “Wait,” “Alternatively,” and “Hmm” during decoding.
Training-free experiments across four models and five benchmarks reduce token use by 18.6%–25.0% while maintaining performance.
Results also report 0.07%–1.48% accuracy improvements and more coherent, concise outputs judged by LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free decoding intervention to reduce overthinking in large reasoning models, relevant to LLM reasoning and efficiency.
papers.title: CALM: Consistency-Aware Logit Masking in Decoding Space for Mitigating Overthinking of Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: CALM reduces large reasoning models’ unnecessary chain-of-thought steps by masking redundant transition tokens while preserving—and sometimes improving—accuracy.

papers.abstract: Automated Gleason grading of prostate whole slide images (WSIs) enables faster and more consistent cancer risk stratification. However, it remains a challenging task due to the subtle morphological differences between grades, the severe class imbalance arising from rare patterns, and the diagnostic features that span multiple spatial scales. Pathology foundation models (FMs) extract strong patch representations but often operate at a single-scale, which limits spatial context and disproportionately affects classes that depend on broader context. The challenge of fusing multiple scales and complementary models, with minimal data and computational resources, remains unresolved. We propose a multi-scale classifier built on state-space models. Our method combines two complementary feature sources: a frozen foundation model, and a lightweight FastVim, pre-trained on ImageNet and distilled from the foundation model, that reads the raw image crops. At each scale, a Mamba model encodes the features from both sources with linear-time spatial context, and a jointly trained head fuses the encoded representations into one prediction. On the PANDA dataset, our method reaches macro F1 of 0.894 and Gleason 5 F1 of 0.802 under 5-fold cross-validation, a 12% and 21% relative improvement over the best single-scale model. A controlled study over 5 foundation models, 5 base classifiers and 3 scales confirms that the gain holds across encoders, with larger improvements observed at smaller scales.
authors: Zihe Zhang, Weimiao Yu, Piumi Don Simonge
bullets: Addresses subtle morphology, class imbalance, and multi-scale context challenges in prostate WSI grading.
Uses frozen foundation-model features alongside ImageNet-pretrained, foundation-model-distilled FastVim features from raw crops.
Mamba encoders provide linear-time spatial context at each scale, followed by joint feature fusion for prediction.
On PANDA with 5-fold cross-validation, achieves 0.894 macro F1 and 0.802 Gleason 5 F1.
Improvements are consistent across tested foundation models and classifiers, with larger gains at smaller scales.
papers.selection_reason: Fuses foundation model features with Fast Vision Mamba for pathology grading. The use of Mamba (state space models) and foundation models is relevant to multimodal foundation models and efficient AI architectures.
papers.title: Multi-scale Fusion of Fast Vision Mamba and Foundation Model Features for Patch-Level Gleason Grading in Computational Pathology
papers.tldr: A multi-scale Mamba-based model fusing pathology foundation-model and FastVim features improves patch-level Gleason grading, especially for rare Gleason 5 patterns.

papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution detection in continual learning (OOD-CL) is highly challenging, as it requires (i) learning a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting, and (ii) identifying unknown samples (OOD) without access to known (in-distribution (ID)) data from past tasks, where standard confidence-based OOD scores tend to degrade. Existing methods largely rely on a rehearsal buffer of past data or assume closed-world settings, limiting their scalability and reliability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel OOD detection framework for rehearsal-free continual learning, inspired by Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), which mitigate catastrophic forgetting via their inherent local neuroplasticity. To better leverage KAN in OOD-CL, we introduce a task-adaptive classifier architecture, TA-KAN, which mitigates recency bias and enhances ID--OOD separability through task-specific control of activation locality. Furthermore, we propose a geometry-guided OOD score that complements TA-KAN classifier confidence without relying on past ID data. Our method significantly improves OOD detection while maintaining strong ID classification performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in OOD-CL.
authors: Nimeshika Udayangani, Flora D. Salim, Christopher Leckie, Sarah Erfani
bullets: Addresses OOD detection when past task data are unavailable and catastrophic forgetting must be avoided.
Introduces TA-KAN, a task-adaptive classifier designed to reduce recency bias and improve ID–OOD separation.
Adds a geometry-guided OOD score that complements classifier confidence without using past ID data.
Reports significantly improved OOD detection with strong ID classification and state-of-the-art OOD-CL results.
Scope: focuses on rehearsal-free continual-learning settings.
papers.selection_reason: Rehearsal-free continual learning with out-of-distribution detection; directly fits continual and online learning.
papers.title: Out-of-Distribution Detection in Continual Learning
papers.tldr: A rehearsal-free continual-learning framework combines task-adaptive KANs with geometry-guided scoring to detect OOD samples while preserving classification performance.

papers.abstract: As physical AI increasingly relies on sensing to understand physical systems, reliable condition monitoring of industrial machinery has become more important. Motors are ubiquitous in industrial systems, and increasing system complexity raises the likelihood of simultaneous faults. Accordingly, compound fault diagnosis that identifies multiple fault components and their severities is increasingly required. Because different fault components jointly affect the same vibration signal, their severity classification can be formulated as related tasks, making multi-task learning (MTL) suitable for exploiting shared information. However, conventional shared-trunk architectures force tasks to share a common representation, potentially causing negative transfer because fault components are characterized by different time-frequency regions. To address this issue, this study proposes a Residual Neural Dimension Reductor with Time-Frequency Channel Attention (RNDR-TFCA), an attention-enhanced cross-talk architecture for multi-output compound fault diagnosis. RNDR-TFCA preserves task-specific feature extractors while selectively exchanging information across tasks. Time-frequency attention emphasizes informative intra-task regions, while channel attention enhances useful inter-task information after nonlinear feature fusion. Experiments on a rotor-bearing system with inner-race fault, outer-race fault, misalignment, and unbalance showed that RNDR-TFCA achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898, outperforming single-task, multi-class, shared-trunk, and cross-talk baselines. Ablation experiments confirmed the benefit of jointly applying both attention mechanisms. RNDR-TFCA required 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs, only slightly higher than RNDR. Channel-expanded baselines still underperformed RNDR-TFCA, indicating that the gain was not simply attributable to increased model capacity.
authors: Wonjun Yi, Wonho Jung, Junho Kim, Rismaya Kumar Mishra, Yong-Hwa Park
bullets: Targets simultaneous identification and severity classification of motor faults from shared vibration signals.
Uses task-specific feature extractors with cross-task information exchange instead of a fully shared trunk.
Time-frequency attention highlights informative within-task regions, while channel attention refines exchanged features.
On a rotor-bearing system, it achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898 and outperformed the evaluated baseline architectures.
Ablations supported using both attention mechanisms; the model used 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an attention-based architecture for diagnosing compound faults in physical motors. Involves sensing physical systems and multi-task learning for physical interaction, relevant to robot learning.
papers.title: Motor compound fault diagnosis using an attention-based cross-talk architecture
papers.tldr: RNDR-TFCA improves compound motor-fault diagnosis by combining task-specific features with selective attention-based information sharing across fault types.

papers.abstract: Large self-supervised speech models provide powerful representations for speaker verification, but full fine-tuning is expensive. Most conventional adapters insert small trainable modules to modify the output of each layer, while keeping the original residual connections unchanged. Building on our preliminary study of manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections in speaker encoders, we explore parameter-efficient adaptation of both residual paths and feature selection across layers. We first propose a Manifold-Constrained Residual Adapter (MCRA), which splits the hidden dimensions of each Transformer residual state into N groups and uses a small Sinkhorn-normalized matrix to exchange information among them. A learnable gate controls the balance between the original and mixed residual paths. The gate adds only one scalar parameter at each residual connection and initially favors the original path, allowing gradual adaptation. We further propose Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation (FALA), an attention-based aggregation method that uses a single learned query shared across all utterances to compute layer weights separately for each speech frame. Because the layer representations depend on the input, the resulting weights vary across both utterances and frames, unlike the fixed weights of a conventional layer-weighted sum. Compared with a frozen WavLM baseline using a fixed layer-weighted sum, our method achieves relative EER reductions of 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb, with trainable adaptation parameters equivalent to only 0.0009% and 0.0016% of the WavLM-Large parameters, respectively.
authors: Zezhong Jin, Xiaoyu Wang, Zhe Li, Chong-Xin Gan, Siqing Qin, Man-Wai Mak, Kong Aik Lee
bullets: MCRA splits residual states into groups, exchanges information using a Sinkhorn-normalized matrix, and learns a gate balancing original and adapted paths.
FALA uses a shared learned query to assign input-dependent layer weights separately for every speech frame.
The method targets efficient adaptation without full fine-tuning of large self-supervised speech models.
Relative EER reductions are 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb versus a frozen WavLM baseline.
Adaptation uses only 0.0009%–0.0016% of WavLM-Large’s parameters, depending on the evaluation set.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient residual adaptation and layer aggregation reduce trainable parameters, transferable to efficient fine-tuning of large models.
papers.title: Manifold-Constrained Residual Adaptation with Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation for Speaker Verification
papers.tldr: A highly parameter-efficient speaker-verification adaptation method jointly modifies residual paths and selects Transformer layers dynamically for each speech frame, substantially reducing EER over a frozen WavLM baseline.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view novel view synthesis (NVS) is essential for AR/VR and real-time communication applications, yet remains challenging when reconstructing 3D scenes from limited viewpoints. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) excels in dense-view scenarios, it suffers from overfitting and geometry degradation under sparse inputs. Current approaches often tackle these problems from a local perspective, addressing either data quality or training regularization individually, lacking a unified and interpretable framework for systematic improvement. We introduce a new perspective that reframes sparse-view 3DGS from a few-shot learning viewpoint, treating each Gaussian primitive as a neuron and leveraging deep learning regularization techniques. Under this unified framework, our approach generates more effective supervision from scarce observations through two strategies: (1) data-related supervision enrichment via optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and joint camera-scene optimization; and (2) training-time regularization via motion-aware dropout and early stopping, which suppress overfitting while preserving dynamic-scene stability. Extensive experiments on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 volumetric video challenge sparse-view dataset demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art optimization-based and feed-forward baselines. Our system won first place in the sparse-view track of the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 challenge.
authors: Lejia Ye, Bin Wu, Jingjing Gao, Yiyang Wu, Xiaohu Zhang
bullets: Reframes each 3D Gaussian primitive as a neuron, providing a unified perspective on sparse-view reconstruction.
Enriches supervision with optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and joint camera-scene optimization.
Uses motion-aware dropout and early stopping to suppress overfitting while maintaining dynamic-scene stability.
Outperforms reported optimization-based and feed-forward baselines on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 volumetric video challenge sparse-view dataset.
Won first place in the challenge’s sparse-view track.
papers.selection_reason: Improves 3D Gaussian Splatting for sparse-view novel view synthesis using a few-shot learning perspective and regularization techniques. This advances 3D foundation models for reconstruction.
papers.title: Rethinking Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting: A Few-Shot Learning Perspective on Overfitting Prevention
papers.tldr: A few-shot learning framework improves sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting by enriching supervision and regularizing training to reduce overfitting and geometry degradation.

papers.abstract: Unlike on-policy distillation (OPD), which depends on a separate teacher model, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a single language model acting simultaneously as the student and the teacher, with the teacher conditioned on privileged information. Despite this architectural simplicity, synchronous rollout generation dominates overall training time, creating a severe systems bottleneck when scaling OPSD. To address this, we introduce Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation (AsyncOPSD), a framework that decouples rollout generation from learner updates to improve training throughput. Since the teacher and student share parameters, AsyncOPSD eliminates the multi-model coordination overhead inherent to OPD architectures in asynchronous training. As the student policy evolves, buffered trajectories generated by older policies become stale, potentially degrading performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a distillation objective based on staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, AsyncOPSD improves the training throughput by $1.96$--$2.25\times$ over synchronous OPSD while increasing average benchmark accuracy.
authors: Xidong Wu, Qi Qi, Yuqiong Ji, Shangqian Gao
bullets: Synchronous rollout generation is a major throughput bottleneck in on-policy self-distillation.
AsyncOPSD decouples rollout generation and learner updates, avoiding multi-model coordination overhead because teacher and student share parameters.
It addresses stale buffered trajectories with staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting.
Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, it achieves 1.96–2.25× higher training throughput than synchronous OPSD and improves average accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Asynchronous on-policy self-distillation improves LLM training throughput by ~2x; reduces training compute/time.
papers.title: Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: AsyncOPSD accelerates on-policy self-distillation by asynchronously separating rollout generation from learner updates while maintaining or improving reasoning accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Recent methods explore step-level signals such as attention mass and step entropy to identify and suppress unnecessary steps. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. Experiments across two model scales and nine benchmarks show that IGPO achieves up to 62% average token reduction and better overall performance among compared methods.
authors: Guanda Li, Xuefeng Bai, Yulong Chen, Zhiyong Wang, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang
bullets: Long reasoning traces often mix useful and redundant intermediate steps.
Existing step signals describe model behavior but not each step’s causal contribution to the answer.
Interventional Step Credit (ISC) estimates step importance through targeted parameter-level interventions.
IGPO uses ISC to rescale reinforcement-learning advantages at fine granularity.
Across two model scales and nine benchmarks, IGPO reduces average tokens by up to 62% while improving overall performance versus compared methods.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces redundant chain-of-thought steps in large reasoning models via interventional step credit, directly relevant to efficient LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Learning to Reason Efficiently with Interventional Step Credit
papers.tldr: IGPO uses causal, intervention-based step credit to shorten chain-of-thought reasoning while preserving important steps and improving performance.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.
authors: Lingsen Zhang, Wei Li, Jie He, Henghua Zhang, Kai Mo, Shiyong Li, Yanpeng Wang, Rui Shao
bullets: Targets the learning burden and semantic-to-action gap in direct vision-language-action policies.
Models actionable state changes instead of reconstructing complete future states, reducing focus on static or irrelevant details.
Combines LT-Filter for local manipulation changes with GT-Anchor for coarse future-direction regularization.
Uses DDAR to inject the learned Delta into action denoising as a structured action-space seed.
Experiments report improved long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization.],
papers.selection_reason: Compact latent delta as actionable transition for VLA robotic manipulation; fits embodied VLA, robot learning, and latent-action world modeling.
papers.title: Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: VLDA learns compact, task-relevant state-change representations to bridge vision-language understanding and reliable robotic manipulation actions.

papers.abstract: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.
authors: Guanghua He, Hancan Zhu, Gaohang Yu, An Zhang
bullets: Targets parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pretrained 3D networks for 36-month MCI conversion prediction.
Learns task-specific proxy updates and approximates them with candidate input/output Tucker rank pairs while preserving spatial kernel modes.
Uses normalized layerwise reconstruction residuals and dynamic programming to find a globally optimal rank allocation under a fixed adapter budget.
On ADNI, achieves mean AUC 0.7706 across five seeds, versus 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning.
Uses approximately 0.618 million trainable parameters, or 1.45% of the full model; evaluation is scoped to ADNI with hippocampal-segmentation pretraining.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning via adaptive Tucker rank allocation under a fixed parameter budget; directly targets training efficiency.
papers.title: Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient MCI Conversion Prediction
papers.tldr: A residual-guided dynamic-programming method allocates Tucker ranks across 3D convolutional layers under a strict parameter budget, improving MCI-to-Alzheimer’s conversion prediction over the compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.
authors: Changshuo Liu, Jiaqi Zhu, Wenqiao Zhang, Xiaokui Xiao, Beng Chin Ooi
bullets: Addresses the gap between sample-level modeling and clinicians’ use of population patterns alongside individual variation.
Uses reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts.
Encodes each patient’s deviation from a cohort prototype as a structured drift signal.
Integrates cohort- and drift-aware representations into a multimodal foundation model.
Shows consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across EHR tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses condition monitoring of physical industrial machinery (motors) using attention-based architectures. Relates to sensing and understanding physical systems, a core aspect of embodied AI.
papers.title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
papers.tldr: CODA improves multimodal clinical reasoning by combining learned patient cohorts with patient-specific deviations from cohort prototypes.

papers.abstract: An evidence-review system must allocate additional model judgments and control their use. We study these software decisions on 6,164 frozen manufacturing source-task pairs. Benefit-targeted routing learns recovered agreement minus newly introduced disagreement. On the original 300-case test, 60 consultations yield 202/231 agreements with two human references versus 189/218 for a logistic-risk router. An additional 300 cases were independently annotated twice using equal frozen evidence. Without retraining the historical policies, the corresponding counts are 164/190 versus 163/193; the differences do not resolve an advantage. Strict scalar-Ridge controls share preprocessing, regularization and fitting, and remain inconclusive. Quotation and requested-state replacement gates retain rejected cases and budget costs; their joint gate rejects one original and two additional consultations without changing primary outcomes. Evidence ablations, fusion and bounded updates supply further controls. A completed 200-pair identity audit yields 97.45 percent weighted merge precision after eight author adjudications. This audits a provisional map, while prospective company-disjoint performance remains untested.
authors: Yijiashun Qi, Hanzhe Guo, Yuxuan Li
bullets: Evaluates consultation allocation and revision controls for LLM-based manufacturing supplier evidence screening across 6,164 frozen source-task pairs.
Benefit-targeted routing models recovered agreement minus newly introduced disagreement when selecting additional model judgments.
On the original test, it achieved 202/231 agreements versus 189/218 for logistic-risk routing; on an independent 300-case set, results were inconclusive (164/190 versus 163/193).
Quotation and requested-state gates preserved rejected cases and budget accounting, rejecting one original and two additional consultations without changing primary outcomes.
An identity audit reached 97.45% weighted merge precision, but this audits a provisional map; company-disjoint prospective performance remains untested.
papers.selection_reason: Applies LLMs to evidence screening in manufacturing. Represents an application of LLMs to a specific domain task, relevant to the general utility of language foundation models.
papers.title: Benefit-Targeted Routing and Bounded Revision for LLM-Based Evidence Screening in Manufacturing Supplier Discovery
papers.tldr: Benefit-targeted routing and bounded revision provide controlled evidence-screening mechanisms, but the routing advantage remains inconclusive and prospective generalization is untested.

papers.abstract: Game world models have made rapid progress toward real-time interactive generation. Yet action control is still predominantly implemented as feature conditioning, leaving the model to learn from training data how each action should move the visual world. This formulation is poorly matched to a broad class of planar-camera worlds, such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, player motion induces a geometrically well-defined planar camera displacement. We observe that the key to spatially consistent control in such worlds is to represent the effect of each action directly in world coordinates. To this end, we introduce ActionRoPE, a parameter-free action interface that converts action-driven camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions. As a result, tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time. These world coordinates further expose a spatial asymmetry in generation: regions covered by the initial observation are geometrically known, while newly revealed regions remain to be synthesized. We therefore propose Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS), which assigns token-wise denoising schedules according to this known-new structure. It allows observed regions to stabilize earlier, while new content is generated with reference to them. Compared with four representative action-conditioning mechanisms, our approach follows the commanded motion more faithfully and reduces the revisit drift by 66% over the strongest baseline. The same interface transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes. Project Page: https://teawhite.cn/ActionRoPE/
authors: Zhiyang Deng, Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Yeying Jin
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feature-based action conditioning, which requires models to learn action-to-motion geometry from data.
Uses a parameter-free interface that converts action-induced camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions, preserving consistent token locations across time.
Introduces Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling to stabilize observed regions earlier while synthesizing newly revealed content using them as reference.
More faithfully follows commanded motion and reduces revisit drift by 66% versus the strongest of four representative baselines.
Transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ActionRoPE, a method for spatially consistent control in game world models by representing actions as world coordinates. This directly addresses action-conditioned generation and controllable world models.
papers.title: ActionRoPE: action as coordinates for spatially consistent control in planar-camera game world models
papers.tldr: ActionRoPE improves spatially consistent control in planar-camera game world models by encoding actions as world-coordinate positional shifts and scheduling denoising based on observed versus newly revealed regions.

papers.abstract: Rollout decoding affects both which trajectories are used for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and how many completion tokens are spent collecting them. We study whether candidate-token support should remain fixed or widen during training in the context of rollout sampling efficiency. Our main schedule moves from top-K=10 to K=20 and then to full support as the attempted-token budget increases. In a 4B code-RLVR setting, the schedule has a higher interpolated 150M-token validation value than its matched fixed-K=10 continuation in all three runs, with a mean gain of $1.80{\pm}0.42$ points. The schedule also performs comparably to a separately trained fixed-K=20 baseline, the strongest fixed-support setting in our sweep. Follow-up experiments suggest that late widening to full support is the most promising variant, although the evidence remains noisy, and mixed-reward-group diagnostics do not clearly explain the gain. An exploratory single-run test replay yields identical point estimates for the schedule and fixed $K=10$. Overall, our results show that rollout support is an important control for sampling efficiency in RLVR and motivate further study of adaptive support schedules.
authors: Zhaonan Li, Zelei Cheng, Amritansh Mishra, Chia-Hsuan Lee, Mann Patel, Sambit Sahu, Ben Zhou, William M. Campbell
bullets: Fixed versus widening candidate-token support is studied for efficient RLVR rollout sampling.
The main schedule increases support from top-K=10 to 20, then to full support as the token budget grows.
In a 4B code-RLVR setting, it outperformed matched fixed-K=10 training across three runs, with a mean gain of 1.80 ± 0.42 validation points at 150M tokens.
Performance was comparable to separately trained fixed-K=20, the strongest fixed-support baseline tested.
Late widening to full support appeared most promising, but diagnostics and a single-run replay did not provide a clear explanation or consistently reproduce the gain.
